Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling’s Christmas tree display is ever so chic, and ever so easy to make yourself using cuttings from your own garden...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling are one of those celebrity couples that keep their heads down and their private lives just that; private. So sue us, then, that we get excited when they offer us a sneak-peek into their world... especially when it comes with a Christmassy twist!

Now, we usually think of a Christmas tree as being larger than life, and twice, especially when it's in the home of a celebrity. Honestly, though, most stars seem to be taking a laidback approach to their festive decor of late, whether it's the Beckhams' bow-filled Christmas tree, Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, or even Michelle Obama's twig tree.

Eva and Ryan have opted for a similarly unfussy approach; the couple's kitchen island is full of miniature Christmas trees. Check it out:

And just like that, they've proven you don’t need a large traditional evergreen tree to make your house look stylish during the holidays. In fact, if you decide to follow in Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's footsteps, you might not need to buy much at all.

All you have to do is take a simple stroll around your garden with a pair of pruners and a small pot to get the same look; fortunately, some experts told me exactly how to do it.

“The best mini Christmas trees start with a walk around your own garden,” says Nick Alan, founder of Palma Botanical Co., who has been growing plants for 25 years.

His picks? “Conifer tips like cedar, cypress, juniper and fir hold their needles longest. Boxwood and rosemary fill gaps and add scent.”

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

For clean cuts, Nick Alan recommends these Fiskars SoftGrip bypass pruners.

Use gentle hands with the shrub, though. “Harvest on a cool morning with clean pruners, cutting just above a side shoot so the plant regrows, and take no more than a third of any shrub,” says Alan.

Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a simple pot method for getting the Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling look this Christmas.

“Fill a 4-inch pot with damp sand (this will help hold your stems upright and will allow you to leave the tree in its pot as it dries). Remove the needles from the bottom 2 inches of each stem (you don’t want any foliage to rot in the sand!).”

Once this is done, she says you should “arrange the stems from tallest in the middle to shortest as you work your way out (creating a cone shape).” Remember, though, that cut foliage won’t last forever. “Mist every few days and keep it away from the stove, dishwasher vent, and sunny windows. Expect two to three weeks, swapping tired sprigs,” says Alan.

A living tree means you don’t have the extra work of worrying about sprigs. “For a kitchen island display like Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling's, I like a living miniature tree best, because it does two jobs at once: it looks festive, and it stays useful after Christmas,” says Morgan Brooks, founder and editor of Plant Style Home.

Brooks says rosemary is the practical pick for a kitchen: “Rosemary is the most practical in a kitchen because you can pick sprigs for cooking, and it smells wonderful near the stove.”

For care, Brooks says: “I keep young trees in cool spots away from radiators and water the compost so it stays lightly damp but never wet.” Alan adds: “Give it your brightest window, water when the top inch is dry, and plant it out afterward in zone 8 and warmer.”

Your kitchen island may be a great spot for trees, but don’t forget it’s also a workspace for cooking. Keep your trees all to one side and never let them near heat sources, especially the dry foliage.

Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, says that “a little greenery with one beautiful ribbon often looks more considered than a crowded arrangement.”

For the layout, Melam says: “I love displaying mini trees in odd-numbered clusters of varying heights. Negative space is key! I’d keep the tallest stem 10-12 inches so as not to compete with faucets, etc.”

A tray helps too: “Displaying them on a tray or wooden slab can help tie them together & unify the display (as opposed to them looking like random pots on a counter).” On a budget, Alan says: “Pine cones, dried orange slices and ribbon dress them cheaply.”

Alan has one note of advice for people with pets or small children: “Skip holly, yew and mistletoe around pets and kids, since all are toxic.”

While Eva Mendes and Ryan Gosling have both played a variety of characters throughout their film careers, we really do think that “people with a stunning Christmas kitchen island” is one we really fancy having a go at, too.

#7886. Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, new pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is important to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

It’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

Whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

The red bracts get all the attention, but the little buds in the middle of a poinsettia say far more about its ability to last the distance over the holidays.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It happens every December. You bring home a full, bright red poinsettia, set it on the table, and a week or two later the colorful bracts start to curl and fall. By Christmas morning, the plant looks tired and half bare.

Some of that can be blamed on poinsettia care after you get home, like a cold windowsill or a pot left sitting in water. Much of it starts at the store, though. The plant was already on its way out before it ever went in the cart.

There's an easy way to tell a fresh one from a tired one, and hardly anybody looks. Forget the red for a second. Down in the center of each cluster of colored leaves are some tiny yellow-green buds, and those say a lot more about how long the color will hold up. It's kind of a strange thing to judge a plant by, but trust the process.

Those colorful "petals" on a poinsettia aren't petals at all. They're bracts, and they color up in fall as the nights get longer. Right in the middle sit the real flowers, small knobby clusters called cyathia. Each one is a little cup holding a single female flower and several male flowers, often with a yellow gland on its rim.

Cyathia go through the same cycle on every plant. They start out tight and green or red-tipped, open to shed yellow pollen, and then drop off. After the cyathia fall, the colored bracts usually follow before long.

Some of the newer poinsettia varieties hang on to their cyathia longer. So it isn't a sure thing, but it's still one of the better clues you get in the store. Any color works for this check, whether you're eyeing red or the pink poinsettias at Walmart (which come in a four-pack for maximum festive joy).

Bend down and look closely at the center of a few bracts. Plants on the same table can be at different stages, so check more than one. Ideally, the cyathia are mostly closed, green or tipped with red, and fresh-looking. Some yellow showing is fine on its own. That's often just the gland on the side of the cup – it doesn't mean the flower has opened.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Now compare that to a plant where the buds have split open and yellow pollen is dusting the bracts below them. If you see that, or you find bare stubs where cyathia used to be, that poinsettia has been blooming a while already. It may look fine today, but it has less time left than the one beside it with tight buds.

Classic red poinsettias come in a four-pack from Costa Farms, and you can order them on Amazon – and the same quick look at the center works on a plant that shows up at the door.

The green leaves under the bracts deserve a look too. Check for yellow leaves low on the stems, or bare spots where leaves have already dropped. Cold, poor light, and watering trouble can all cause that. Pass on a plant that droops or looks wilted, along with any that have torn, bruised, or creased bracts. Bluish or whitish edges on the bracts can be a sign of cold injury.

Flip a few leaves over as well. Whiteflies, such as the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), are common on poinsettias, and a puff of tiny white insects lifting off when you brush the plant is a bad sign.

Lift the pot if you can. Soggy soil in a heavy pot may mean it's been sitting in water inside its foil, and roots kept that wet can rot. Pay attention to where the plants are displayed, too. Poinsettias crowded by the automatic doors can catch a blast of cold air every time the doors open, and plants left packed in plastic sleeves for days can droop and drop their flowers early – ethylene gas builds up inside the sleeve.

When you get home, use a soil moisture meter, like the Xlux moisture meter available on Amazon, to take the guesswork out of watering.

The journey home is where poinsettias tend to get hurt. When it's below 50°F (10°C) outside, sleeve or wrap the plant before it leaves the store, even for the short walk to the car. Just a few minutes of cold air can damage the bracts and leaves, and the damage may not show right away. Save the garden center for your last stop so the plant isn't stuck in a cold car while you're in other stores, and warm the car up first. Once you're inside, get the sleeve off pretty quickly.

Pick a bright room for your poinsettia. Keep the plant near a window but out of hard, direct sun, and well clear of heat vents, the fireplace, and any door that lets in a draft.

Normal house temperatures work fine, roughly 65 to 70°F (18 to 21°C) during the day, with nights around 60°F (16°C) or a little warmer. Window glass gets cold at night, though, and so can the air right beside it. Set a digital indoor thermometer, like the TempPro TP50, for a night or two, and you'll know for sure.

Stick a finger in the pot before you water. If the top of the soil is dry, go ahead, and if it's still damp, wait a day or so. That shiny foil holds water like a bowl, so poke a few holes in the bottom, or take the pot out and water it over the sink until it drains. A ceramic planter, like this Garden & Home Red 8 Inch Indoor Ceramic Plant Pot, with drainage holes and saucer, is a much nicer option than foil anyway. You don't need fertilizer while a poinsettia is in bloom.

Pick a plant with tight little buds in the center, keep it somewhere warm and bright, and the color can hold for weeks after the holidays. So the next time you're standing in front of a whole table of red, skip past the brightest one for a second and look at the center first.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7883. Think Winter Kills All the Wasps in Your Yard? Here's Where Next Year's Queens Are Hiding

Wasps seem to vanish once the cold sets in, but not all of them are gone. Next year's queens are tucked away close by, and a few of their hiding spots might surprise you.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After the first hard frost, the wasps that pestered every picnic in August are suddenly gone. It's easy to figure the cold finished them off. So where do wasps go in winter, and do wasps die in winter at all? Most of them do – just not the ones that count for next year.

Before you look up how to kill wasps next spring, know that yellowjackets, paper wasps, and hornets live in colonies that last just one season. Each colony leaves behind young queens that have already mated and will ride out the cold on their own.

Some of the places where wasps hide in winter are right in your yard. Firewood, loose bark, and the gaps around a shed door can each hold a queen until spring.

For the common social wasps, the colony only lasts a year. Each spring, a single queen starts a small nest and raises the first workers herself. The colony grows through summer, and by late summer it switches to raising males and new queens. The new queens mate in fall, then leave the nest for good.

Everyone else is left behind. By the time hard freezes settle in, the old queen, the workers, and the males have died, and the papery nest sits empty for good. The mated queens are the only ones that make it into winter, and they don't go back to the nest. Each one finds its own sheltered spot. Many still won't last until spring, but the ones that do will start the whole thing over.

Here are some of the common places you'll find queens hiding.

Rake back a deep drift of oak leaves in midwinter, and the ground underneath is often softer and less frozen than the open lawn. Yellowjacket queens may crawl into that leaf litter or under old mulch and pulled plants at the edge of a bed. They stay perfectly still. You'd likely never notice one. Some leaves left in place also help butterflies and moths overwinter, and there's no reason to rake every corner bare because of wasps.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Stacked firewood is full of narrow gaps out of the wind, and rotting logs and old stumps offer soft wood a queen can tuck into. Pull a few splits from the bottom of the stack in winter, and you may find one clinging to the bark, too cold to move much. Check each piece before carrying it inside – a warm living room can wake a dormant queen. Bring in only what you'll burn that day. Walmart's leather palm work gloves are tough enough for sorting through the stack.

Loose bark on a dead tree makes a snug pocket. Yellowjacket queens squeeze into those gaps. Birds have a hard time reaching them there, and the bark keeps off most of the weather. On a mild winter day, try lifting a slab of it off an old stump. You could find a queen pressed flat in the gap underneath, barely moving. Put the bark back if you do. She isn't going anywhere until spring.

Sheds, garages, and barns are full of cracks around door frames and window trim. Queens often move in during fall and stay put until spring. Paper wasps tend to seek out high spots for the winter, and they sometimes overwinter in clusters, packed together at the peak of a roof or along a rafter. To keep queens from slipping in next fall, cover open vents with stainless steel mesh, which Amazon sells in small sheets.

Queens find their way into wall voids and attics through gaps where siding meets trim, or through cracks around windows. Temperatures in there usually stay above freezing. Ever find a slow, groggy wasp on a window inside the house in January? It's usually a lone queen that wandered in from the walls, drawn toward the light. An active nest looks different – steady traffic in and out of the same hole in summer or early fall points to a live colony inside the wall.

Don't plug that hole while the nest is active, since the wasps may chew through to the inside. Once the colony has died off, seal exterior cracks with a flexible sealant such as DAP Dynaflex 230 from Home Depot.

Some yellowjacket queens spend the winter underground, but not in the nest they came from. That old nest is abandoned when the colony dies, and it isn't used again. She might use an empty mouse or vole burrow instead, a crack between rocks, or a small pocket in loose soil.

A home compost pile that hasn't been turned in a while is another possibility. If you turn the pile in winter, move slowly and wear gloves, and she'll probably stay put.

Usually, there's no need. Wasps are useful predators. Yellowjackets and paper wasps hunt caterpillars and other soft-bodied insects to feed their young, and the adults visit flowers for nectar, moving some pollen around as they go. A queen sleeping under a log at the back of the yard poses little risk, and next summer her colony will probably eat a good number of garden pests.

Doors, windows, and play areas are a different story. Seal gaps around the house in late summer, before queens go looking for winter shelter, and check that window screens fit tightly. Home Depot carries a door jamb weatherstrip set that closes the gaps around exterior doors.

Once spring warms up, glance at the eaves and porch ceiling every so often. A brand-new nest is about the size of a golf ball, and only the queen is tending it, so it's far easier to handle than a full colony in August. Large nests, ground nests, and anyone in the house who's allergic to stings are a job for a pest control professional.

In winter, the yard looks empty, but not entirely. Somewhere under those leaves or behind that bark, next year's wasps are sitting out the cold. Unless one is tucked in beside the back door, it can stay right where it is.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7882. GPOD on the Road: Shakespeare Garden in Evanston, Illinois

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

Earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

While wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

The garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

The garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

Jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

Last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

The Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.

#7881. The Best Combination Squares for Accurate Layout and Repeatable Marks

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 20, 2026 12:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

A combination square earns its keep before the first cut, helping woodworkers and DIYers mark straight crosscuts, check corners, lay out miters, and repeat measurements. We tested seven of these versatile measuring tools to find out how accurately they measured and whether their blades stayed put once locked.

A small layout error can carry through a project, leaving joints that won’t close or parts that don’t align. Our Best Overall pick, the Starrett 11H-12-4R 12-Inch Steel Combination Square, delivered accurate results in our squaring and miter checks, and its blade held its setting during our retention test. Its hardened-steel blade and fine graduations make it a strong choice for detailed layout work.

Our tested picks include compact woodworking squares for small jobs, longer models for wider workpieces, and options with useful extras. Read on for our hands-on findings and the features to consider when choosing the best combination square.

Whether you’re choosing tools for building the essential toolbox or adding a specialized square to your workshop, these tested picks cover a range of sizes, materials, and features.

The Starrett 11H-12-4R combines a 12-inch hardened-steel blade with a cast-iron head for checking square, laying out miters, and transferring measurements. Its photo-engraved 4R graduations run from eighths down to sixty-fourths of an inch, and the head includes a bubble level and scribe. A reversible lock bolt allows the blade to be secured in either orientation.

We were impressed with its accuracy in our layout tests. After scribing a fine line against a straight factory edge, we flipped the square and scribed again from the same starting point; the lines aligned. The 45-degree face also checked out when we marked opposing angles and checked that they formed a right angle. We checked the blade against a manufactured straightedge and used a light behind it to look for gaps. Its graduations also agreed with our reference steel rule.

Just as important for repeated measurements, the blade held its setting after we tightened the lock and gently tapped the tool. That secure hold means less need to stop and recheck a setting between marks. The inch-only scale is a limitation for metric work, and the cast-iron head deserves careful handling to protect its measuring faces. For users working in fractional inches, however, the Starrett delivers an accurate layout and dependable blade retention in our tests.

What our tester says: “I was really impressed by how closely the lines aligned in my flip test and how well the blade held its setting after gentle tapping. The quality of this square is obvious.” –Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Starrett combination square at Amazon or Zoro.

For small projects, a 6-inch combination square is just right. This Ace square offers a stainless steel blade, a machined cast-zinc head, and both inch and metric markings in a compact package. It’s a good option for homeowners who need to mark short crosscuts, check corners, or transfer measurements. Its size also makes it a practical choice to keep in a toolbox for quick repairs.

We put the Ace through the same accuracy checks as the larger squares, and it performed well. Its squaring and miter faces passed our opposing-line tests, and the ruler markings matched our reference steel rule. The blade also passed our straightness and light-gap checks. Once secured, it resisted movement when we gently tapped it—a useful result for anyone making several marks at the same setting.

The included screw-in scribe and bubble level add versatility without requiring separate accessories. We also like having millimeters alongside fractional inches. The main compromise is reach: the short blade won’t extend across wider stock, and its finest inch divisions are thirty-seconds. We’d consider it for small layout jobs or as a companion to a longer square.

Get the Ace combination square at Ace Hardware.

A combination square needs to hold a measurement as reliably as it establishes one, and the Mr. Pen delivered on that requirement in our tests. We tightened its spring-loaded brass bolt, gently tapped the tool, and checked the setting again. The blade hadn’t crept, giving us confidence in its ability to maintain an offset for repeated marking. Its 12-inch stainless steel blade provides useful reach for general woodworking layout, while the included brass scribe and bubble level round out the basic features.

Accuracy was also good across our checks. The ruler agreed with our reference steel rule, and we found no issues when checking blade straightness against a manufactured edge and looking for gaps against a flat surface. Both angle faces performed well, too: the reversed square produced matching scribed lines, and opposing marks from the 45-degree face formed a right angle. These results support using it for everyday tasks such as marking crosscuts, checking assembled corners, and laying out miters.

The blade carries inch and centimeter scales, with fractional-inch divisions in eighths, sixteenths, and thirty-seconds. That selection covers many common layout measurements, although users who work in sixty-fourths will need a finer rule. We’d consider the Mr. Pen for a general-purpose woodworking kit, particularly when secure blade retention and a full-length rule matter more than extra-fine graduations.

Get the Mr. Pen combination square at Amazon or Mr. Pen.

The Milwaukee MLSQC12 adds a magnetic head to the familiar sliding-square design, giving it applications beyond wood layout. Two rare-earth magnets are designed to hold against steel and other ferrous materials, making the square an option for users who also work with conduit or metal stock. Its larger head provides more contact with the workpiece, while machined 45- and 90-degree faces handle squaring and miter layout.

We checked those working faces rather than assuming the additional features meant better accuracy. The Milwaukee passed both flip tests, producing aligned square lines and opposing 45-degree marks that formed a true right angle. Its 12-inch blade also checked straight, and the graduations agreed with our reference steel rule. We paid particular attention to blade retention: after setting and tightening the draw bolt, we gently tapped the square and found that the measurement held. That matters when transferring the same dimension to multiple pieces.

Other features include a precision-etched stainless steel blade, a Sharpsite bubble vial, and a scribe pin stored in the head. A scribe hole at the 1-inch mark provides another layout option. The magnetic feature has an obvious material limitation—it won’t hold to wood, aluminum, or other nonferrous surfaces—but the square remains usable conventionally on those materials. We’d consider this model for a workshop that handles both woodworking and steel layout.

Get the Milwaukee combination square at The Home Depot, Acme Tools, or Zoro.

The Irwin 6-inch metal combination square comes with a cast-zinc head, a stainless steel blade, and black precision-etched scales. That construction gives it the familiar features of a larger workshop square in a shorter format. We’d reach for this square when laying out small parts or checking narrow stock, where a longer blade can extend unnecessarily beyond the workpiece.

In testing, the Irwin handled the essentials well. We verified the ruler against our reference steel rule and checked the blade for straightness and gaps against a flat surface. It passed those checks, along with our tests of the square and miter faces. We also found that tightening the blade lock kept the setting from shifting even after gentle tapping. For repeated measurements, that secure adjustment is every bit as important as having an accurate scale.

The main limitation is the blade’s reach. Six inches is useful for close layout work, but it won’t span the same material widths as a 12-inch square. We’d keep the Irwin available for smaller measurements and corner checks, then use a longer model when the job calls for extending a line farther across a board.

Get the Irwin combination square at Amazon and Acme Tools.

WorkPro pairs two useful layout tools in this combination square set: a 7-inch rafter square for angle marking and a 12-inch combination square for adjustable measurements. The tools serve complementary purposes. The rafter square’s lipped fence registers against a board’s edge, while the combination square’s sliding head lets users establish depths and offsets. For someone assembling a woodworking tool kit, having both expands the range of layout jobs the set can handle.

We concentrated our accuracy testing on the combination square, which has a die-cast zinc-alloy head and a matte stainless steel blade. Its ruler matched our reference steel rule, and the blade passed our straightness and light-gap checks. The 90- and 45-degree faces also produced the expected results in our flip tests. After tightening the adjustment screw, we gently tapped the tool and checked for blade movement; the setting remained unchanged.

The combination square includes a metal scribe and bubble level, plus scales with sixteenth-inch, thirty-second-inch, and millimeter divisions. Users needing sixty-fourth-inch measurements will want a finer rule. The separate aluminum rafter square adds a fixed layout tool that can also serve as a crosscut guide. We’d consider this set for general carpentry projects that call for both adjustable measurements and quick angle layout.

What our tester says: “I like having a rafter square and an adjustable combination square together for framing layout tasks. The WorkPro square passed all accuracy checks and held its setting securely.” –Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the WorkPro combination square set at Amazon or WorkPro.

When a standard 12-inch square won’t reach far enough across a workpiece, the iGaging’s 24-inch blade provides another foot of working length. That extra reach makes it worth considering for wider boards, shelving, and furniture components. We’d choose this size for projects where extending a layout line farther from an edge is necessary.

A longer blade makes straightness particularly important, so we checked the iGaging against a manufactured straightedge and looked for light gaps against a flat surface. It performed well in both checks, and its ruler markings agreed with our reference steel rule. The angle tests were also spot-on: reversing the square produced aligned scribed lines, while opposing marks from the miter face formed a right angle. We also checked whether the blade would creep after tightening the lock and gently tapping the tool. It retained its setting, supporting consistent measurements between marks.

The trade-off is handling and storage. A 2-foot blade needs more clearance around the workpiece and more room in a drawer or tool cabinet. For small parts or crowded work areas, we’d keep a shorter square nearby. The iGaging makes the most sense as a dedicated tool for larger layout jobs.

Get the iGaging combination square at Amazon.

We tested seven combination squares, evaluating ease of use, accuracy, readability, durability, and value. To check each square’s 90-degree face, we registered its head against a straight factory edge, scribed a fine line, then flipped the square and scribed again from the same point, checking for divergence. We tested the 45-degree faces by marking opposing angles and checking whether they formed a true 90-degree angle.

We compared blade straightness against a manufactured straightedge and held each blade against a flat surface with light behind it to reveal gaps. We also checked ruler graduations against a trusted steel rule. To test blade retention, we tightened each lock, gently tapped the tool, and rechecked its setting. These checks informed our accuracy assessments; we also considered adjustment, scale legibility, construction, included features, and price when evaluating the squares.

A combination square pairs a sliding ruler with a head for checking 90- and 45-degree angles, measuring depths, and marking consistent offsets. Understanding squares, levels, and plumbs can help you compare different types of squares and their applications. Compact models suit small parts, while longer blades extend across wider workpieces. Some sets add center-finding or protractor heads, and magnetic models provide holding assistance on steel.

Blade length determines how far a combination square can measure or mark from an edge. A 6-inch model suits small parts, narrow stock, and confined spaces. A 12 inch combination square offers a practical balance of reach and handling for general woodworking, while 18- and 24-inch blades accommodate wider boards and larger components.

A combination square’s usefulness depends on the relationship between its blade and head. The blade should be straight, the graduations correctly spaced, and the working faces accurately set at 90 and 45 degrees. Fine scale divisions alone don’t establish accuracy; a detailed ruler cannot compensate for an out-of-square head.

Check a new square before relying on it. Register the head against a known straight edge, draw a fine line, then flip the square and draw again from the same point. Diverging lines indicate a problem. Keep contact surfaces free of debris, and repeat the check after a drop or impact that could affect alignment.

Look for a blade with crisp, easy-to-read markings in the units and increments you use most. For standard woodworking, 1/16-inch graduations are often used for general layouts, while 1/32-inch divisions are crucial for making tight fits in trim and moldings. If you’re more familiar with metrics, you’ll want to choose millimeter markings.

Squares with etched markings tend to be more expensive, but they also hold up better than printed markings that can wear off with repeated handling. Dark markings on satin-finished blades can be easier to read under bright shop lights.

For reliable combination square use, the blade should slide smoothly when the lock is loosened and remain fixed when tightened. Binding makes small adjustments frustrating, while excessive play can prevent the blade from seating consistently. Check that the head sits firmly against the workpiece without rocking and that the adjustment knob is easy to grip.

Check a new square before relying on it. Register the head against a known straight edge, draw a fine line, then flip the square and draw again from the same point. Diverging lines indicate a problem. Keep contact surfaces free of debris, and repeat the check after a drop or impact that could affect alignment.

These answers explain how to use a combination square, check its accuracy, and keep it working properly.

A combination square is a measuring and layout tool with a ruler that slides through an adjustable head. The standard head provides 90- and 45-degree working faces, allowing the tool to check corners, mark miters, and measure depths or offsets.

Rest the head firmly against a workpiece’s edge to mark or check 90- and 45-degree angles. Slide and lock the blade to measure depths, check heights, or mark consistent offsets. The removable blade also serves as a ruler. If included, the bubble vial checks level, and the scribe scratches fine layout lines.For checking level over longer distances, use a dedicated level suited to the job. Our guide to the different types of levels explains the options and their applications.

Accuracy varies by model and manufacturing tolerances. A straight blade, accurately machined head, and secure lock all contribute to reliable results. Fine graduations don’t guarantee accuracy, and price alone doesn’t establish it. Check any new square before use and recheck it after a drop or impact.

Use a board with a known straight edge. Hold the square’s head firmly against that edge and draw a fine line along the blade. Flip the square, register the head against the same edge, and align the blade with the line’s starting point. Draw again. The lines should coincide; any divergence indicates a squareness error, assuming the board’s edge is straight and the tool is seated correctly.

To set the blade, loosen the locking knob, slide it to the desired measurement, and retighten. If the square appears inaccurate, remove the blade, clean its groove and the head’s contact surfaces, then reassemble and repeat the accuracy check.Calibration procedures vary by design. Some squares permit correction at the blade’s seating surfaces, but filing or sanding removes material permanently and can worsen the error. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions or seek service or replacement if cleaning doesn’t resolve the problem.

Wipe away dust, moisture, and debris after use, paying particular attention to the blade groove and locking mechanism. Dry the tool before storing it, and apply any lubricant or rust protection according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Avoid abrasives on the graduations and measuring faces. Store the square where its blade won’t bend, and protect the head from drops and impacts.

Hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away. Shea McGee, however, has made a point of doing the opposite, and to beautiful effect!

That's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree! And, much like Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, it's one of those oh-so-simple but oh-so-effective ideas that we can't believe we didn't think of first.

A post shared by McGee & Co. (@mcgeeandco)

As you can see above, Shea McGee has decorated her tree with warm brown, tan, and cream ornaments, dried orange slices, clip-on LED candlesticks, and dried hydrangeas from her own garden (although you can buy ready-to-go cone hydrangeas from McGee & Co if you prefer an easier life).

It's a beyond brilliant idea, as it means the blooms get a second act, which is a better return than most shrubs give you. If you want a similar look, just read on for some tips from the experts.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Keen to give it a whirl from scratch? Look this way...

Cameron of DreamHowYouLive favors Limelight (the same as Shea McGee grows) and Annabelle for a hydrangea arrangement. “Their petals dry stiff and papery, so they keep their shape, where softer mopheads crumble.”

Flower farmer-florist Joey McFarland of Flowers by Dr. Jo agrees that panicle types like Limelight are best for long stems. He warns that bigleaf hydrangeas set buds in fall, so cutting too deeply means “cutting off your blooms for next year.” Shopping for plants? Browse our list of panicle hydrangea varieties.

Timing is highly important as well, especially when it comes to hydrangeas. Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home waits until the heads “turn papery and antique in early fall.” Cut too soon and, as Cameron warns, “they wilt instead of drying.” (Which means you need to show patience, grasshopper).

When it comes to drying hydrangeas the experts all have a different opinion, which tells you how difficult it can actually be. Floral preservation artist Nadi Melam of Florals Memories says, “I always dry hydrangeas in a vase of water,” about an inch, for a “lovely muted antique color.”

Cameron hangs them upside down in a dark, dry spot for two or three weeks, since vase-dried heads “tend to droop.” Our guide to drying hydrangea flowers covers both.

The best rule to follow if you want the Shea McGee effect? Water-drying holds shape and color well, while air-drying is quicker but leaves blooms more fragile.

There’s one place where most people go wrong when drying hydrangeas for Shea McGee-style decor. As Cameron tells me me he cuts the head town to 3-inch stems, wires each branch and tucks the whole bloom into a gap. His personal rule: “Three small clusters spread around the tree look intentional. One big bunch at the top looks like a mistake.”

Arslan Ali of DecoroDea advises, “Treat them like picks, not ornaments,” and says to place them last, “after the ornaments and lights are already on,” so you fill the gaps that are actually still dark. Brooks wires clusters low near the trunk first, then moves smaller heads toward the tips. In essence, you can take a bit from every expert tip.

For McGee’s look, add dried orange slices, cream and tan ornaments, and warm white lights. Bright white, Cameron notes, makes “the whole thing look cold.”

Dried petals shed, which is why Melam is so blunt with their advice: “You lose petals every time you touch a flower.” Cameron’s fix is a light hairspray mist that “keeps the shedding down.” And, as for those annoying relatives, who “just want to adjust one thing,” tell them that your Shea McGee-inspired Christmas tree is now a museum exhibit, so hands off".

If you don't have real hydrangeas in your yard, faux hydrangeas as a no-mess alternative. These cream-white stems give the same soft look without the shedding.

Hydrangeas are also toxic if chewed, so keep clusters out of reach of curious pets.

Those candles on Shea McGee’s Christmas tree? Make them LED.

Melam says, “Open flame is a no-no since the dry material will ignite right away.” As for saving them for next year, the experts are once again split.

Want a warm glow like MsGee's but without the fire risk? These warm white, dimmable clip-on LED candles come with a remote, so you can keep real flames far from your dried hydrangeas.

Melam stores heads flat in a box with tissue between layers, and Cameron has reused the same heads two years running. However, McFarland says dried blooms “won’t do particularly well in storage” and suggests composting them and cutting fresh ones.

Either way, it’s a good excuse to plant more hydrangeas and see what tip works best for you.

#7878. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options

Looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

Understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden

Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

Even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build new nests.

The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

#7877. This is the Right Height for Mounting a TV on the Wall

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Manasa Reddigari, Theresa Clement, Phillip Tinner

Updated Nov 20, 2026 2:12 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

How high you should mount a TV on the wall is a question that stumps binge-watchers and cinephiles alike. Position the TV too high or low, and you’ll have to crane your neck or slump your shoulders to take in the on-screen action. A misplaced TV can also be a pain to remove and reinstall at another height, which is why it’s in your best interest to get it right the first time.

Manufacturers and home entertainment enthusiasts recommend mounting a TV at eye level for optimal viewing, but the best TV height for you also depends on TV wall mount type, screen size, and other factors. The answer to how high should a TV be mounted sometimes varies slightly for those reasons, but these rules of thumb will help you come to the right decision.

As you think about how high to mount a TV, most experts use the center of the TV screen as the main point of reference, no matter the screen size. Unless you’re mounting a TV for just one person to use, keeping the center of the TV at a comfortable viewing height for most people should be the goal. Forty-two inches from the floor to the center of the screen is the ideal TV mount height under most circumstances.

For tailored comfort, however, you can actually factor your height, and the height of fellow household members, into your TV’s height from the floor. You’ll find a more exact center point for your TV mount by measuring the distance from the floor to each household member’s eye level when sitting. Add those measurements together and divide by the total number of people for your bespoke TV wall mount height.

Note that while TV size doesn’t always affect mounting height, a TV’s dimensions matter when considering optimal viewing distance. If you have a large, 65-inch or 75-inch TV, it may be uncomfortable to watch if your seating is too close to the wall it’s mounted on, regardless of how high or low it’s mounted. In these and similar cases, use a TV mount height calculator to simplify the math and guesswork involved in determining the best TV viewing distance and height for your space.

These LED strip lights connect to your TV’s USB port to light up your screen from behind. See our full review.

Not all of the seats in a living room are going to be the same height. An open floor plan with counter-height bar stools, bar-height stools, and a sofa, for example, can complicate TV mounting height. Counter-height bar stools are higher off of the floor than sofa seats—anywhere from 24 to 29 inches to reach the counter. Bar-height stools are even taller, at 29 to 33 inches.

If the seats in a room are at various heights, or the room in question isn’t a living room, consider the following approaches.

There are several other spatial and functional considerations to account for when determining the position and height of a wall-mounted TV. In your home, these may include:

When thinking about how high to hang a TV, you shouldn’t position it so high that viewers need to tilt their heads up more than 35 degrees from eye level in order to see the top of the screen, according to the Society of Motion Picture & Television Engineers.

Tilting a TV’s screen downward is one way to position it higher than eye level without causing discomfort or neck strain, if necessary. This requires upgrading from a basic low-profile mount (which is stationary) to one of two other types of TV mounts: a tilting wall mount (which can move up or down) or full-motion mount (which can swivel in all directions). For a full walkthrough of how to install either type of mount, check out our guide on how to mount a TV to the wall.

Deciding where to mount a TV on the wall can be confusing. Televisions are heavy and expensive items, so it’s important to get it right on the first try. Knowing how high to mount your TV depends on a few factors, and keeping the center of the screen at eye level is the most critical. While professional TV mount installation is always an option, careful measurements and the above tips will get your TV properly positioned for a comfortable premiere.

#7876. What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

Why Are My Houseplant Leaves Dropping Off in November?

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Snake plants tolerate a lot of neglect, but November is different. Shorter days, cold windows, and indoor heating all call for a change of routine.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say. But that changes in November. The days get short, and the heat comes on, and the watering habit you kept all summer now leaves the potting mix wet for weeks. Yellow leaves and soft, mushy bases tend to follow.

Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right. Once light levels drop, your snake plant isn't growing much, so it uses far less water and needs no fertilizer at all. What it does need is a dry pot between drinks, steady room temperatures, and a spot out of the cold air that pools along windows.

Take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks. Run through them now, then again on a gray afternoon in December. That alone considerably cuts the odds of losing a snake plant to winter.

Don't rely on a calendar when watering snake plants. A snake plant that needed water every two weeks in July might go a month or more between drinks in November. Its surface won't tell you much. So how do you know when it's dry? Push a finger down as far as it goes, or try the chopstick trick: push a wooden skewer to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. Damp mix clings to the wood and darkens it; dry mix leaves it clean.

If you're struggling to know when to water, then use a moisture meter for an accurate assessment, like the Xlux instant read probe, available from Amazon. Water only when the whole depth comes up dry, then let the pot drain fully. Leaves that go soft or flop over at the soil line usually mean the roots have sat wet too long.

Low light is something a snake plant tolerates, not something it grows well in. In November, the sun sits lower and the days are short, so a dim corner that was fine in June may now get very little light. Growth slows, and the mix stays wet far longer because the plant is barely drawing water.

A spot within a few feet (about a meter) of an east or west window helps. Make the move gradual, though – a plant that goes straight from a dim hallway into hours of direct south sun can scorch.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Without a bright window, a grow light like the Sansi Pot-Clip-On Grow Light, positioned a foot or so (30 cm) above the leaves, fills the gap.

On a cold evening, hold the back of your hand near the window where your snake plant sits. Chilly on your skin means chilly on the leaves, too. Blame single-pane glass, the gap under an outside door, or a nearby heating vent. Any of them can swing the temperature more than a snake plant can take – even while the thermostat reads fine.

Ordinary room temperatures are what you're after, roughly 60–85°F (16–29°C). Trouble starts if the plant sits below about 50°F (10°C) for long stretches. Leaves pressed against cold glass can develop soft, water-soaked patches. So at night, pull the pot back a foot or two (30–60cm) from the window.

If you want to see what the plant goes through after dark, then use a high/low thermometer, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer, which displays both high and low temperature and humidity levels.

Tip the pot and look underneath. Drainage holes get plugged with compacted mix, a stray pebble, or roots that have grown through. In a decorative cachepot, a snake plant can stand in an inch (2.5 cm) of old water without anyone noticing. Lift it out and check. If the mix is still wet a week or more after you watered, it may have broken down and is holding too much moisture.

Winter is a poor time to disturb roots, so repotting snake plants is normally a spring job. The exception is a pot that won't drain at all – or a mix that stays soggy no matter what. Then a careful repot now beats rotting roots in March. For a replacement, choose a pot with a drainage hole and its own saucer, like this Vigoro ceramic planter from Home Depot. Fill it with a gritty potting mix, like Miracle-Gro Cactus, Palm, and Citrus Mix, which drains much faster than regular potting soil.

Look each leaf over, down to the soil line, for signs of common snake plant problems. If yellow is creeping up from the base and the leaf feels soft or mushy there, you're looking at overwatering and rotting roots. Cold damage can look a lot like it, though. Wrinkled or curling leaves usually mean the reverse: the plant went too long between drinks.

Next, check the crevices where leaves overlap for pests. Cottony white tufts there are mealybugs (Planococcus citri), and small tan or brown bumps that stay put when nudged are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Dab a few with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow up with a ready-to-use insecticidal soap, like Garden Safe insecticidal soap, sprayed right onto the insects. It's far easier to deal with a dozen now than hundreds in February.

Put the fertilizer away until spring. A plant that isn't actively growing can't use the feed, so unused salts build up in the mix and can burn roots. Hold off on routine repotting for the same reason. Fresh mix and a bigger pot push a plant toward new growth right when the light to support it is lowest. Disturbed roots also recover slowly in a cool room.

Don't water your snake plant on a schedule just because the heat is drying out the air. Dry air and dry soil aren't the same thing, and a snake plant copes with dry air far better than it does with wet roots. For the next few months, you want it holding steady, not growing.

Run the same five checks again around the new year. In winter, a snake plant mostly needs the right spot and to be left alone. Give it that, and the one looking a bit tired in November is usually putting up new leaves by late spring.

Given a kitchen’s function as a social space, transit zone, food prep and cooking hub, and display area for decor, it’s probably one of the trickier rooms to light properly. Proper illumination also makes it easier to stow or retrieve items in and under cabinets high or low, allows you to slice and dice with greater safety and precision, and can even make a kitchen look and feel larger.

While many homeowners cite a lack of natural light as the reason their kitchens are dim, artificial lighting of the wrong type or in the wrong location can make the problem worse. When you’re revamping your kitchen lighting design, it’s smart to assess everything from function and fixture to the type of light bulbs you use. Ahead, find solutions to common kitchen lighting challenges to ensure the best kitchen lighting for all your needs.

A solid kitchen lighting strategy should ideally have fixtures in all of the following categories:

A layered approach helps minimize shadows, which often result from the exclusive use of overhead lighting, and glare, which can stem from only using bright task lighting.

The VyanLight Motion-Sensor LED Lights are easy to install and ideal for brightening dark areas. See our full review.

Look for the best fixtures in each of the three lighting categories:

Certain LED light fixtures, such as LED strips, cast a beam of light onto a surface that is brightest and most concentrated at the center of the beam and less bright on the edges. This is suitable for countertops made of butcher block, stone, or another material with a flat or matte finish. But with marble, granite, or similarly glossy materials, the center of the beam can produce a distracting glare even when placed a few feet away from it. To avoid this, place LED light strips inside light housings, which are aluminum channels with frosted covers that help diffuse bright light and minimize glare on shiny kitchen surfaces.

Incandescent, compact fluorescent light (CFL), and LED light bulbs for the kitchen come in one of three color temperatures that describe the color characteristics of the light the bulb emits. There’s Soft White (2700K to 3000 Kelvins (K)), Cool White/Bright White (3500K to 4100K), and Daylight (5000K to 6500K). The higher the bulb temperature, the cooler (i.e., bluer) the light it emits; the lower the temperature, the warmer (i.e., more amber) the light. Choose the color temperature best suited for the function of the fixture:

Remodeling your kitchen to include a natural ambient light source such as a skylight or one or more windows can lend extra warmth to the room and fill any gaps in the light coverage of your artificial light fixtures. Even in a packed kitchen, there will often be vacant spots where you can install a window, including:

Providing effective and attractive kitchen lighting is simply a matter of layering appropriate lighting types into your kitchen lighting design. Plan out and install the right mix of ambient, task, and accent lighting and your space will be well-lit and safe. With the right kitchen ceiling lights, your beautiful new space will be ready for festive gatherings with family and friends.

For safety and functionality, you’ll want lights that provide ambient and task light. Depending on your setup, you may also need accent lighting to highlight special features in your space. Be sure to find lights that are properly rated for the wet, potentially grimy environment of a kitchen.

First determine the functionality of the lighting you need. Then consider the decor of your home and which style of light fixture is the best match. Pricing, too, may be a factor, as there is a wide range of prices associated with lighting and you’ll want to select kitchen light fixtures that align with your budget.

Choose a fixture that emits adequate lighting for your environment, and select one that complements your design style.  You’ll likely have to peruse lots of web stores to find the kitchen chandelier that’s just perfect for your space, but the effort is worth it.

Your Thanksgiving feast could provide a few tasty treats for garden birds. Just make sure you know which leftovers are safe to serve and which should stay off the menu.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they? Before throwing everything into the compost or bin, though, take a look at your Thanksgiving leftovers; your feathered friends could be very thankful for them!

Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).

Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...

Before we dive on in, a word of caution: not every Thanksgiving dish is suitable for wildlife, especially as salt, butter, rich sauces and seasonings can make seemingly harmless scraps unsuitable for birds.

The trick? Try to save a few simple ingredients before they make their way into the casserole dish or onto the dinner table. With that caveat in place, then, here are seven Thanksgiving kitchen scraps worth keeping...

Have a few apples left over from your Thanksgiving preparations? Birds such as robins and other fruit-eating visitors will definitely appreciate small pieces of fresh apple.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Cut the flesh into bite-sized chunks, removing the core and seeds first. Bruised apples are fine so long as they're fresh (they're not as fussy as we are!), but discard any mouldy or spoiled pieces. And avoid offering apple pie filling or cooked apples covered in sugar and spices.

Cranberries are a Thanksgiving staple, and you'd better believe that their fresh (and unseasoned, obviously) counterparts make a lovely treat for birds. Offer a few whole or chopped cranberries on a clean feeding tray like this one from MIXXIDEA.

Frozen cranberries are fine, too, once thawed. Just avoid cranberry sauce, as it typically contains added sugar and may include other ingredients birds don't need. Honestly, a little fresh fruit is all that's required.

Pecans (again, plain and unsalted) are another holiday favorite that can be shared with feathered visitors, along with walnuts and peanuts. All of these scrummy nuts are rife at Thanksgiving, and all provide fats and protein that can help birds maintain their energy during colder weather.

Take care to chop larger nuts into manageable pieces and check that they haven't been coated in salt, sugar, chocolate or seasoning. Just like the fruit, nuts should be fresh, too, rather than stale or musty.

Corn often features on the Thanksgiving menu in a big way, and a few plain kernels can be offered to garden birds; just set aside a small portion before adding butter, salt or other seasonings.

Cooked or fresh corn kernels can be placed on a feeding tray, but avoid creamed corn, buttery corn casserole and heavily seasoned dishes. Only offer a little at a time, as damp corn can spoil quickly.

If pumpkin or squash features in your holiday cooking (or your Thanksgiving decor, if you're Kristin Davis!), don't throw away all those seeds; instead, rinse away any stringy pulp, remove any seasoning and allow the seeds to dry thoroughly.

Offer them (have I gotten too repetitive yet?) plain and unsalted, either whole for larger birds or broken into smaller pieces for smaller visitors. They're a useful source of fats and nutrients, making them a worthwhile addition to your bird feeding station.

Leftover rice can also be shared with birds from your Thanksgiving feast, provided it hasn't been cooked with salt, butter, oil, garlic or onions. Both white and brown rice are suitable in small quantities when prepared plainly.

P.S. There's a persistent myth that uncooked or cooked rice swells inside birds and causes harm, but this isn't true. Nevertheless, rice shouldn't replace more nutritious bird food, so just offer just a small amount (you may find your birth month winter bird adores it) and remove anything uneaten so it doesn't have a chance to go bad.

A little leftover boiled or baked potato from your Thanksgiving prep can be another treat for your feathered friends. Set aside a portion before adding butter, milk, salt or gravy, then allow it to cool and chop it into small pieces.

Please never offer raw potatoes or green potato peelings, and avoid chips, roast potatoes cooked in fat and heavily seasoned mashed potatoes. Experts always advise that plain potato be treated as an occasional extra rather than a regular food source.

It's every bit as important to know what to avoid when it comes to feeding birds your Thanksgiving leftovers. Turkey fat and pan drippings might seem like an easy substitute for bird suet, but they're best kept off the feeding station. Audubon, in fact, warns that turkey fat melts more readily than traditional suet and can turn rancid quickly. It can also smear onto feathers, potentially affecting their waterproofing and insulation.

Gravy, stuffing and salty side dishes should also stay off the menu, as they often contain butter, salt, onion and garlic, none of which are suitable additions to a wild bird's diet. Avoid, too, anything that contains chocolate, along with avocado, sugary desserts and heavily processed foods, too. Bread and pastry aren't particularly nutritious (even if they won't do any harm), so think up some better ways to use your leftovers; might this author humbly submit the idea of a bread-and-butter pudding?

Once you've picked all of the bird-friendly scraps out of your Thanksgiving feast, be sure to present it properly! Always use a clean feeding tray rather than leaving piles of food on the ground, and try to put food out in the morning, as this is when it's most likely to be eaten.

Take care to remove anything uneaten before it spoils, and wash feeding surfaces regularly to reduce the risk of bacteria and disease spreading. It's also worth keeping fresh drinking water available, particularly as colder weather approaches, and remember that kitchen scraps are supposed to be occasional extras, not a replacement for a balanced wild bird food mix.

Still, all those warnings aside, there's no denying that sharing a little of your holiday feast with your local birds is a lovely way to give thanks to Mother Nature (and reduce food waste at the same time).

#7873. Your Compost Pile Needs These 6 Things Before Winter If You Want to Make Black Gold Through the Cold
