#7744. A Pro-Life Progress Report for the 119th Congress and the Administration

Four years ago, the Supreme Court corrected a grave legal error and overturned Roe v. Wade. With abortion no longer enshrined as a “right” in the Constitution, policymakers at all levels of government have stepped up to promote life in law, policy, and culture. For the first session of each new Congress, The Heritage Foundation provides pro-life policy recommendations to Members and the presidential Administration. The following year, a progress report takes stock of what has been accomplished and what remains on the to-do list. Last year, President Donald Trump and a Republican majority in Congress took the reins. Heritage provided a pro-life policy road map of ways to reverse four years of President Joe Biden’s pro-abortion radicalism.[REF] Now, this Backgrounder analyzes legislative and administrative accomplishments and highlights additional ways the Administration and Congress can protect life.

In Congress

From appropriations to the reconciliation process, the 119th Congress protected taxpayers from supporting abortion and abortion businesses.

Legislation

Congress advanced important legislation to promote a culture of life.

Defunding Big Abortion. Congress’s signature pro-life victory in 2025 was the One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB) budget reconciliation measure. It included a provision preventing abortion providers like Planned Parenthood from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for one year.[REF] Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s annual federal funding sources. In 2025, more than 50 clinics closed their doors, and across the country Planned Parenthood clinics are feeling the financial strain.[REF] Some blue states have stepped in to try to supplement funding but this is not sustainable in the long run.[REF] Both Planned Parenthood and blue state Attorneys General went to court to try to block the defund provision from taking effect, but were ultimately unsuccessful.[REF] Congress holds the power of the purse, and nothing in the Constitution entitles the abortion industry to Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars. As discussed below under “More to Accomplish,” another reconciliation bill could allow the defunding provision to extend beyond the OBBB’s one-year time frame, which has already passed. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF]

Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Students. In January 2026, the House of Representatives passed the Pregnant Students’ Rights Act (H.R. 6359),[REF] which requires universities to provide pregnant women and girls with information about their rights, resources, and available accommodations.

Pregnancy Resource Center Support. Also in January 2026, the House also passed the Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Women and Families Act (H.R. 6945),[REF] which provides statutory clarity that states can direct Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funding to pregnancy resource centers that support mothers, families, and unborn children through services like counseling, material support, and education.

Addressing Weaponization and Selective Enforcement. The House Judiciary Committee approved the FACE Act Repeal Act (H.R. 589)[REF] in June 2025. The bill is needed in light of intense weaponization by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) under President Biden, which is also discussed below. The Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (FACE) Act[REF] was enacted in 1994 and prohibits physically obstructing, injuring, intimidating, or interfering with anyone “obtaining or providing reproductive health services.” Under President Biden, the DOJ deliberately targeted peaceful pro-life Americans while failing to vigorously enforce FACE Act protections that apply to churches and pregnancy centers, which faced increasing attacks following the Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. Sufficient laws already exist at the state level to address criminal activity, so Congress should repeal the FACE Act once and for all.

Appropriations

Congress stood firm to protect life via spending legislation.

Maintaining Status Quo of Pro-Life Policies. House-passed appropriations legislation has incorporated numerous pro-life policy riders, such as the Hyde family of amendments that prohibit taxpayer funding for abortions in foreign and domestic programs. However, new pro-life policy riders are routinely stripped during negotiations between the House and Senate.[REF]

Addressing Problematic Earmarks. In FY 2024, two hospitals that perform late-term abortion procedures received almost $2.5 million in federal funds via earmarks in that year’s Labor-HHS [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services] funding.[REF] Those were Senate earmarks; the House Labor–HHS subcommittee accepted no earmark requests for FY 2024 through FY 2026.[REF] For FY 2027, the House Appropriations Committee’s Labor–HHS subcommittee provided guidance for earmark requests.[REF] Among requirements going forward, entities that perform or promote abortions are not eligible. Entities that conduct research using embryonic stem cells obtained from an induced abortion, or human germline gene modification, are not eligible. And entities that facilitate sex-rejecting interventions are not eligible.

In the Trump Administration

The Trump Administration played a significant role in advancing pro-life policies.

Previous Executive Orders and Policies

In 2025, the Administration quickly acted on a host of policies, which are discussed in the 2025 Backgrounder.[REF] They include:

  • An executive order to disentangle taxpayers from abortion funding.[REF]
  • Reinstatement of the Protecting Life in Global Health Assistance policy, which disentangles foreign aid dollars from international nongovernmental organizations that perform or promote abortions.[REF] As discussed in the following section, the policy has since been expanded.
  • Defunding of the United Nations Population Fund over its complicity with China’s coercive and inhumane population-control practices.[REF]
  • Renewal of membership in the Geneva Consensus Declaration, a partnership of more than 40 countries committed to improving women’s health, protecting innocent life, and strengthening the family.[REF]
  • Partial restoration of Title X family planning program funding to Oklahoma[REF] and Tennessee.[REF] These pro-life states were denied funding by the Biden Administration over their refusal to provide abortion counseling and referrals.
  • Recission of a Department of Defense abortion travel policy that made travel and transportation allowances available to service members and their dependents for abortions.[REF]
  • Rescission of Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) guidance that wrongly claimed that EMTALA requires doctors to perform elective abortions.[REF]

Pro-Life Regulations, Executive Orders, and Other Policies

Over the past year and a half, the Trump Administration has taken additional steps to promote life-affirming policies. These steps include:

  • Taxpayer Funding for Abortions. In July 2025, the Department of Justice issued an opinion[REF] that the Hyde Amendment, which prohibits taxpayer dollars from paying for elective abortions, means that the HHS cannot spend taxpayer dollars to provide “ancillary services necessary to receive an abortion”—such as the Office of Refugee Resettlement providing transportation for women seeking an abortion. The HHS has said it is reviewing the relevant regulations and guidance.[REF]
  • Abortion in Obamacare Plans. On December 9, 2025, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) issued guidance[REF] about Section 1303 of the Affordable Care Act’s abortion coverage accounting gimmick. Section 1303 requires insurers to collect a separate payment for certain abortion coverage in qualified health plans approved to be sold on the exchanges. Maryland and other pro-abortion states attempted to commandeer excess funds remaining in abortion surcharge accounts to establish grant programs to pay for additional abortion travel and elective abortions.[REF] The CMS clarified that the leftover funds belong to insurers—not states seeking to subsidize additional abortions.
  • As discussed below under “More to Accomplish,” the CMS should re-issue the Section 1303 regulation from President Trump’s first term. In December 2019, the CMS adopted a rule[REF] interpreting that separate payments be just that—separate—and that issuers needed to comply with the letter and spirit of Obamacare requirements. The same has not been true under Presidents Barack Obama and Biden. The CMS should rescind the Biden rule and return to the rule in place during President Trump’s first term.
  • Abortion at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). On December 18, 2025, the DOJ issued an opinion[REF] that the Biden Administration overstepped its authority by issuing a regulation requiring abortion procedures, referrals, and counseling to veterans at VA medical facilities. The VA quickly issued a memorandum returning to pre-2022 policies that excluded abortion and abortion counseling.[REF] On December 31, the VA issued a final rule formally rescinding the 2022 Biden Administration rule that returned to the pre-2022 abortion exclusions.[REF]
  • International Abortion Funding. In January 2026, the Trump Administration announced that it is further expanding life-affirming foreign aid policies. Since the 1980s the Mexico City Policy has required (under Republican Administrations) foreign nongovernmental organizations to certify that they will not perform or promote abortion as a condition of receiving U.S. family planning assistance. During President Trump’s first Administration, that policy was expanded to apply to more funding streams and called the Protecting Life in Global Health Assistance Policy. Now, under a new name. the Promoting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance (PHFFA) Policy has expanded to encompass abortion,[REF] radical gender ideology,[REF] and diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI)[REF] policies as well.
  • Fetal Tissue Research. In January 2026, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) reinstated a policy from President Trump’s first term ending support for unethical and obsolete research using fetal tissue obtained from elective abortion. The prohibition applies to internal and external projects (such as grants to outside entities). [REF] The NIH can prioritize ethical alternatives instead.
  • Planned Parenthood COVID-19 “Relief” Funding. In January 2026, the Small Business Administration (SBA) announced that it is reviewing whether Planned Parenthood affiliates improperly received more than $88 million in loans during the COVID-19 pandemic. The SBA is demanding that Planned Parenthood clinics either prove that they were eligible to receive Paycheck Protection Program loans or return the funding.[REF] During President Trump’s first term, the SBA preliminarily concluded that Planned Parenthood affiliates were not eligible to receive these loans that were meant to help small businesses, but the Biden Administration later forgave many of those loans.[REF]
  • Department of Justice Weaponization. In April 2026, the DOJ issued an extensive report detailing how the DOJ under President Biden weaponized the FACE Act against pro-life Americans.[REF] The report concluded: (1) The DOJ violated Americans’ rights through biased enforcement; (2) the DOJ collaborated with pro-abortion organizations to track pro-life activists’ activity; (3) prosecutors repeatedly engaged in inappropriate conduct; (4) the DOJ sought harsher punishment for pro-life activists than for pro-abortion activists; and (5) the DOJ inappropriately tried to help a pro-abortion organization with an application for a grant.
  • Reviewing Human Embryonic Stem Cell Research. In January 2026, the NIH announced a pause on submissions to the NIH Human Embryonic Stem Cell Registry and issued a request for information on ways to reduce—and potentially replace—current reliance on research using human embryonic stem cells.[REF]
  • Pro-Life Budget Request for FY 2027. In April 2026, the Office of Management and Budget released its budget request for the upcoming fiscal year. The request includes long-standing provisions in current law, such as Hyde protections across multiple departments (foreign and domestic), conscience protections, and bioethics-related funding restrictions for certain research. Additional requests include protections separating foreign aid funding from organizations that perform or promote abortions, including additional conscience protections for medical trainees, stripping Planned Parenthood of any HHS funding, and ending funding for fetal tissue research.[REF] This proposal is a request and Congress will ultimately decide FY 2027 funding and dollar amounts. As with the FY 2026 request, the Administration demonstrated its strong commitment to pro-life policymaking throughout the government.
  • Redirecting Teen Pregnancy Prevention Funding to Align with Pro-Family Priorities. In June 2026, the HHS canceled most federal Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program grants two years early, some of which had gone to comprehensive sex-education curricula taught by abortion providers like Planned Parenthood. The HHS opened new funding opportunities that will be available to grantees who align programming with the Administration’s priorities of sexual risk avoidance education and not encouraging, normalizing, or promoting sexual activity for minors.[REF]

Conscience Rights

The Trump Administration is prioritizing enforcement of federal conscience protection laws. The HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) is ensuring that no person or organization is discriminated against over their convictions on abortion and gender ideology.

In January 2026, the OCR announced a list of enforcement actions and policy changes, including:

  • A notice of violation determining that the Illinois law requiring abortion referrals violates the Weldon and Coats–Snowe Amendments.[REF]
  • A nationwide “Dear Colleague” letter summarizing federal health care conscience protections that the OCR is tasked with enforcing and reaffirming the Administration’s commitment to protect individuals and organizations from being discriminated against due to their sincere moral or religious convictions.[REF]
  • Recission of Biden Administration guidance that wrongly claims that federal law on emergency medical care requires doctors to perform elective abortions.[REF]
  • Recission of Biden Administration guidance that wrongly instructed pharmacies to stock and dispense dangerous abortion pills, even though pharmacies and pharmacists have a right to not violate their conscience by participating in abortion. Under President Biden, the HHS walked back part of this guidance after losing a court case to pharmacies challenging the guidance.[REF] Now the guidance has been rescinded entirely.[REF]
  • Disavowal of[REF] the Biden Administration’s August 2021 decision to withdraw the Trump Administration’s 2020 Notice of Violation that California broke federal conscience rights law over its insurance coverage mandate for elective abortion.
  • Disavowal of[REF] the Biden Administration’s July 2021 decision to withdraw the Trump Administration’s Notice of Violation that the University of Vermont Medical Center broke federal conscience rights law by requiring a health care professional to participate in an abortion procedure despite strong objection.

In March 2026, the HHS announced that the OCR is investigating 13 states over possible violations of the Weldon Amendment, which says government cannot discriminate against health care entities that do not pay for or provide coverage of abortions.[REF] The states under investigation have abortion coverage requirements for plans sold in their respective jurisdictions.[REF]

In May 2026, the HHS announced an additional reorganization within the OCR.[REF] The OCR is tasked with enforcing federal civil rights laws related to conscience, religious freedom, privacy, cybersecurity, and more. In 2018, during President Trump’s first term, the HHS created a Conscience and Religious Freedom Division within the OCR. Under President Biden, this division was shuttered and absorbed, with the Civil Rights Division, into the Policy Division.[REF] Rights of conscience and religious freedom are not “less than.” Restoring the Conscience and Religious Freedom Division will provide the OCR with the tools it needs to best serve all Americans and ensure that their fundamental rights are respected.

More to Accomplish

Both Congress and the Administration have successfully advanced important pro-life policies, but there is still more work to do.

In Congress

Defunding Big Abortion, maintaining long-standing pro-life policy riders, and holding bad actors accountable must continue to be a priority.

Planned Parenthood. Preventing Planned Parenthood and other abortion providers from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for one year was a signature accomplishment in the 2025 OBBB budget reconciliation package. Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s federal funding sources. However, this defunding provision was the only one in the entire bill subject to a one-year time frame rather than the full 10 years to which the bill can apply. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF] If Congress discusses another reconciliation bill, the defunding provision should be incorporated for the full 10-year time frame so that taxpayers do not have to continue funding abortion providers.

Appropriations. Congress has continued to include long-standing riders like the Hyde Amendment and similar language in annual appropriations bills, prohibiting taxpayer dollars from paying for most abortions. But many other pro-life policies can be enacted via appropriations riders. From expanding conscience protections to reinstating commonsense safety protections for risky abortion pills, there is more that Congress should do to promote life in must-pass spending legislation.[REF]

Oversight. Congress should continue to invoke its oversight and investigatory role to hold bad actors accountable and ensure that that pro-life priorities in the Administration are not sidelined. For example, in 2022, activists obtained the remains of five preemie-size unborn babies who had been aborted at a notorious Washington, DC, late-term abortion mill. According to expert testimony, these babies may have been aborted using the illegal partial-birth abortion technique. One baby was still in the amniotic sac and may have been born alive and left to die.[REF] Local authorities stonewalled questions from Congress and the press about any investigation of this activity. Pro-life activists and Members of Congress feared that the DC Office of the Chief Medical Examiner would destroy the five bodies, but in February 2024 it confirmed that it would not immediately do so.[REF] During a June 2025 hearing, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi indicated that there was an ongoing investigation.[REF]

Demand FDA Action on Dangerous Abortion Drugs. Congress should continue demanding transparency from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on its long-promised comprehensive review of the abortion pill. It is abundantly clear that current FDA postmarketing safety policies are not adequately protecting women and children.[REF] In light of the politicized approval process that put this risky drug on the market in the first place, a complete and thorough review is long overdue. Leadership changes at the FDA should not slow down or deprioritize this important work. Individual members and congressional committees should continue emphasizing the dangers these drugs pose to women, girls, and unborn children.

In the Trump Administration

The Trump Administration should rescind Biden-era regulations and policies that promoted abortion and sought to undermine the 2022 Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. These include:

  • Abortion Travel for Unaccompanied Illegal Alien Children (UACs). A senior Office of Refugee Resettlement official told The Daily Signal[REF] that the agency is working on reversing a Biden-era regulation allowing taxpayer-funded abortion travel for UACs.[REF] The changes were submitted to the Office of Management and Budget’s Regulatory Information Service Center in January 2026, but the updated regulation has not been formally proposed yet. The HHS should ensure that the rule advances quickly.
  • A Privacy Regulation That Undercut Abuse Reporting. In June 2025, a federal court struck down[REF] most of a Biden Administration regulation that purported to strengthen protections for sensitive private health information, including information related to abortion. In reality, the rule improperly limited state child abuse reporting laws.[REF] The HHS should formally rescind the rule.
  • The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) Wrongful Interpretation of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). In 2024, the EEOC issued rulemaking interpreting the PWFA’s definition of “medical condition” related to pregnancy to include elective abortion, thus requiring employers to provide accommodations like time off from work to have an abortion or time off to recover from the procedure.[REF] Litigation related to the entire rule is ongoing. In May 2025, a federal court provided nationwide relief for employers who care deeply about the well-being of their employees (and their children, born and unborn) by vacating the elective abortion accommodation provision.[REF] The EEOC should clean up the mess and formally rescind its erroneous interpretation of the PWFA. Pro-life Members of Congress would not have supported this bipartisan bill if it empowered the federal bureaucracy to invent a requirement for abortion accommodations.
  • A Rollback of a Conscience Protection Regulation from President Trump’s First Term. The Biden Administration partially rescinded[REF] President Trump’s 2019 rule about enforcing more than a dozen federal laws that protect conscience rights for individuals or entities that do not want to participate in or facilitate morally fraught procedures such as abortion.[REF] The Biden rule gutted the HHS Office for Civil Rights’ ability to adequately enforce conscience laws that protect Americans’ civil rights. The regulation from President Trump’s first term should be restored.
  • Addressing Title X Family Planning Program Funds Used as a Slush Fund for the Abortion Industry. The Biden Administration rescinded a regulation from President Trump’s first term that required recipients to physically and financially separate all abortion activity from Title X activity and prohibited Title X projects from promoting or referring for abortion.[REF] The Biden regulation also required sites that do not offer a broad range of contraception to provide a prescription or referral. This created a new barrier for sites that offer fertility awareness-based methods (FABMs) but cannot in good conscience provide or refer for other methods. The Title X program should not be used as a slush fund for abortion providers. The Trump Administration should restore the regulation from President Trump’s first term.
  • A Clean Up of Policies Concerning the Affordable Care Act’s (ACA) Nondiscrimination Provision. Among other things, Section 1557 of the ACA prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, age, disability, and sex in covered health programs or activities.[REF] Just weeks after the Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade, the Biden Administration moved to redefine conditions related to “sex” to include abortion, as the Obama Administration had also done in 2016. The Trump Administration should revive the abortion-related provisions of this regulation from President Trump’s first term, issued in 2020.[REF]
  • Ensuring that Issuers Comply with ACA Abortion Rules. Thirteen states require plans sold on their marketplace to include coverage for abortion. Section 1303 of the ACA says that such plans cannot use federal funds (including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions) for elective abortions. Section 1303 also requires issuers to collect a separate payment from each enrollee for the abortion coverage portion and segregate those funds in separate allocation accounts solely used for abortion coverage. Plans are also required to provide notice to enrollees at the time of enrollment that the plan includes abortion coverage. But under Presidents Obama and Biden, CMS policy was essentially an accounting gimmick that did not enforce the letter or spirit of the ACA. The CMS should re-issue the Section 1303 regulation from President Trump’s first term. That rule[REF] rightly required that separate payments be just that: separate.
  • Stopping Elective Abortions in the Indian Health Service (IHS) Program. The Biden Administration issued a rule that weakens the prohibition on abortion funding within the IHS.[REF] Per the Hyde Amendment, federal funds cannot be used to pay for abortion except in very limited circumstances. Under the Biden rule, if Congress ever fails to include the Hyde Amendment in annual appropriations legislation, then the IHS would be able to fund elective abortions.
  • Robustly Enforcing Federal Conscience Protection Laws. Laws like the Church, Coats–Snowe, and Weldon Amendments are meant to ensure that no one faces discrimination for declining to perform, participate in, or pay for an abortion in HHS-funded programs. Under previous Administrations that prioritized a radical pro-abortion agenda, conscience protection was not a priority. The Trump Administration is reversing that trend. The HHS and the OCR should continue to protect Americans from discrimination in federally funded programs. For example, a February 2026 letter to the HHS from Alliance Defending Freedom identifies 49 HHS-funded family medicine residency programs that, it says, violate federal conscience laws by requiring residents to participate in abortion training.[REF]
  • Prioritizing Health and Safety at the FDA and Department of Justice, Not the Abortion Industry’s Bottom Line. The FDA should expeditiously conduct its long-promised review of the abortion drug mifepristone and revisit the dangerous drug’s approval. At a minimum it must restore commonsense safety protections like in-person evaluation and dispensing. To that end, the DOJ also has a role to play in addressing mail-order abortion pills. For starters, it should rescind the Biden-era memorandum[REF] about interpretation of the Comstock Act, which prohibits mailing any “article or thing designed, adapted, or intended for producing abortion.”[REF] As explained in a Heritage Foundation Legal Memorandum, the Office of Legal Counsel’s interpretation of Comstock is so narrow “that it would be virtually unenforceable…. The plain and ordinary meaning of [Comstock] unambiguously prohibits mailing abortion drugs.”[REF]

Pro-Life Progress Is Possible

Slim Republican–Democrat margins in Congress left little room for error when it comes to any legislative priority, including pro-life policies. That is why tools like budget reconciliation and must-pass appropriations legislation are so critical to advancing protections for babies and mothers.

The Trump Administration has steadily rolled back much of the damage wrought by the Biden Administration, but key priorities are still unfinished. With the President’s second term in full swing, pro-life Americans expect to see policymakers continue to deliver more meaningful protections for women, girls, and unborn babies.

Melanie Israel is a Visiting Fellow in the Richard and Helen DeVos Center for Human Flourishing at The Heritage Foundation.

#7743. The Veteran’s Example for America

Veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service. It is also a reminder that freedom depends on citizens willing to serve something larger than themselves—and not just when they are in uniform.

Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.

Across generations, American veterans have answered the nation’s call in war and peace out of a commitment to duty, sacrifice and country. Their example shows that citizenship carries responsibilities as well as rights, and that self-government endures only when citizens place the common good above personal interest.

The freedoms that Americans enjoy today were secured by all veterans who served. They defended not merely our borders but also the principles upon which this nation was founded: liberty, representative government and the rule of law.

By defending the constitutional order, veterans helped preserve a nation in which political differences are settled through lawful debate and elections rather than force. Veterans Day is an opportunity to recognize the men and women whose sacrifices have made that peaceful self-government possible.

>>> The Three Values That Are the Real Keys to America’s Greatness

Veterans have helped secure liberty against some of the most oppressive ideologies in human history, including communism and national socialism. American veterans were instrumental in defeating the Nazi regime during World War II, helping liberate Europe from a government built on tyranny, aggression and the systematic denial of human freedom.

During the Cold War, generations of American servicemen and women stood watch against the expansion of Soviet communism, preserving the security of the free world through deterrence and steadfast resolve. Their service helped create the conditions that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the liberation of millions of people in Central and Eastern Europe.

The freedom enjoyed today by nations once trapped behind the Iron Curtain is part of the legacy of those veterans who answered their country’s call.

Across these conflicts, American veterans served as guardians of the principle that free people have the right to govern themselves. Veterans Day also reminds us that liberty is never self-executing. The constitutional freedoms secured through military sacrifice endure only when citizens practice the discipline, responsibility and respect for law that self-government requires.

The veteran’s example therefore reaches beyond the battlefield, offering a model for preserving freedom in civic life.

Veterans also participate in freedom’s defense at home at some of the highest rates in American society. According to the 2025 Veterans Civic Health Index, 81% of veterans were registered to vote in the 2024 election, compared with 74% of nonveterans. Seventy-three percent of veterans cast ballots, compared with 66% of nonveterans.

The index also reports stronger veteran participation in volunteering, in civic organizations and in engagement with public officials and community institutions. Together, these measures point to a broader pattern: For many veterans, military service becomes a lifelong commitment to citizenship, civic responsibility and the preservation of our constitutional republic.

Veterans continue to serve as teachers, business leaders, first responders, elected officials and civic volunteers, bringing military habits of integrity, discipline and teamwork into civilian life. At Military.com, Medal of Honor recipient Clint Romesha captures that enduring impulse, saying, “So many of us veterans just want to continue to serve after service.”

Mr. Romesha identifies teamwork as one of the military’s greatest lessons—“It’s not about me; it’s about the team”—and as a principle that continues to guide veterans long after they leave the uniform behind.

The veteran profiles of “American Heroes: Stories of Service” and “Pledge to Patriots” show this continuing commitment in action. These stories feature veterans mentoring young people, supporting one another, leading nonprofits, responding to disasters and strengthening communities.

>>> Nina and the Bikers

Thousands of veterans serve as poll workers, election officials and observers, helping to administer and safeguard elections. As a former election official and U.S. Navy veteran, I have seen them step forward when communities need poll workers. Through the nonpartisan Vet the Vote initiative, more than 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers during the 2024 election cycle, up from approximately 63,500 during the 2022 midterms.

National Guard members have supported election operations, security, coordination and emergency response at the request of state authorities. Their commitment to duty, adherence to procedures and record of public service can strengthen confidence in the electoral process they defended in uniform.

On Veterans Day, we honor those who wore the uniform in defense of our nation. We should also follow the example they continue to set—as citizens, poll workers, community leaders and public servants—reminding us that freedoms secured on far-off battlefields must be preserved through faithful participation in self-government at home.

Veterans Day recognizes a profound commitment to country, but it also challenges every American to accept the duties of citizenship.

#7742. My New Book Chapter on How to Curb Dangerous Emergency Powers

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Now avaialble on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver, and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power.

My forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these issues, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of new legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

I recently covered related issues in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7741. Economic Freedom and Educational Opportunity

Education policymakers around the world often overlook a simple formula: To increase educational opportunity, increase economic development.

But to improve development, a country needs the institutions that promote it. That’s why nations that want to help more children succeed should pursue economic freedom.

The latest Economic Freedom of the World report from the Fraser Institute tells the story clearly. The highest-ranked 25% of countries for economic freedom dramatically outperform the lowest-ranked 25%. Incomes are seven times greater, while people work six fewer hours per week. People live 14 years longer. Fewer children die in infancy, and environments are cleaner.

Economic freedom translates into education and economic opportunity. Fewer students in developing nations will drop out in middle school to go to work. More families will be able to afford transportation to school. There will be more opportunities for graduates to get more productive, higher-paying jobs.

>>> Latin America Shifts Toward Market-Oriented Conservatism

Take, for instance, Kurdistan in Iraq, which is focusing more on education now. Iraq ranks 159 out of 165 countries for its legal system and property rights, 152 for size of government, 141 for sound money, 149 for regulation of the economy, and 129 for freedom to trade internationally.

Imagine how many more students in Kurdistan could finish school with a great education if incomes were seven times higher. Imagine the hard trade-offs today that would not be necessary if Iraq were richer.

This point holds worldwide. What would best help a country’s children receive a strong education in the long run? Focus first of all on the country’s economic and legal institutions.

Education is about making plans for society’s future. That means a small government with reliable courts, sound money, secure property rights, and free competition.

Economic development doesn’t automatically mean more government funding for government schools. In many countries, it can mean trusting families with education dollars to choose what is best for their own children.

Indeed, parents are a great education resource. They are the first line of influence to keep their children on track for success, and you don’t even have to pay them a salary.

Governments can do more to consider how to empower parents and teachers. Families know their own children the best. Teachers know their own students as individuals far better than a national government or the United Nations or UNICEF could ever know them.

Using international aid to push an ideological agenda is the wrong policy. Education policy choices should emphasize local knowledge rather than national and international one-size-fits-all, top-down impositions.

>>> Stablecoins Strengthen the Dollar and Empower the Developing World

Educators also should teach economic and financial literacy. The scientific evidence is decisive that socialism fails and market economies succeed. We mark Nov. 7 each year as Victims of Communism Day in the United States by remembering the more than 100 million people who died of starvation or were killed under communist and socialist regimes in the 20th century.

On an individual level, each student should be taught the basics of economics and entrepreneurship. These lessons include the fundamentals of human action and incentives, supply and demand, and the invisible hand of Adam Smith. This also includes learning how to be alert to opportunities to create value for others in society while improving one’s own life.

This education means respecting and admiring entrepreneurs. Students should understand why people should be allowed to keep the fruit of their own labor. Students also should understand the value of building capital rather than consumption if they want to prosper.

To prepare students for employment and participation in society, teach economics and inspire entrepreneurship and an entrepreneurial mindset. Then the next generation will better understand the institutional reforms needed to help their country thrive.

Given the results of the latest U.S. election, now that new policymakers with socialist leanings (and actual socialists) will govern in states such as Michigan, New York, California, and elsewhere starting next year, this advice is not just for other countries. It’s also for us. Will we listen?

#7740. Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:

[W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed new limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing new terms for future cooperation in any event….

[But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a new state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "issue orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

Our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

We also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

Judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

#7739. The Unexpected Source of Muslim Immigration to France

The ongoing riots in France have once again brought the world’s attention to large enclaves of Muslim immigrants in and around the country’s overcrowded housing projects. But foreign observers may be surprised to learn how many of the most recent arrivals came in through the tiny Balkan nation of Slovenia, which enabled a mass migration in 2022-2024. The dynamics of how and why this happened in Europe are well worth our attention in America because, mutatis mutandis, they also obtain along our own southern border. Think of Mexico as our Slovenia.

In 2023, I spent four weeks visiting eight of the countries involved in the transit routes to learn why they had come back to life. What I learned has profound implications for American policy. Led by pioneering member state Hungary, the E.U. had erected a solid barrier along its eastern frontier. But then another member state—Slovenia—elected a liberal government with lax enforcement policies. And that single breach in the defenses left interior countries like France vulnerable once again.

Almost three years have passed since I discovered (and reported) the Slovenia breach in what had been for the previous seven years an effective barrier erected by the European Union. The E.U. effectively put an end to Europe’s catastrophic mass migration crisis of 2014-2016, during which both refugees and terrorists were able to travel freely along the so-called “Balkan Route.”

The Slovenia gap, as I’ll call it, helped flood France with at least 466,000 first-time foreign national asylum and refugee claimants from mostly Muslim-majority nations in 2022-23 alone. Many of these were fast-tracked into the public housing communities now at the center of France’s continuous street violence.

>>> France Is Learning the Hard Way What Happens When the Socialist Bill Comes Due

The flow of migrants began in mid-2022 with a key Slovenian election and spiked in 2023 before declining in 2024. Much of the traffic moved along the same Balkan routes traveled by some 800,000 to 900,000 mostly Muslim immigrants during the 2014-2016 crisis, during which there were an estimated two million illegal E.U. border crossings.

The 466,000 migrants who applied for French asylum or refugee status in 2022-23 hailed from places like Afghanistan, Turkey, Syria, and Tunisia, as well as Muslim-majority nations in North Africa. Of those, authorities detected approximately 244,000 who traveled on routes through the Balkans; untold thousands more are believed to have traveled those same routes undetected. Among those who registered were France-bound immigrants like an Afghan I interviewed in a Bosnian migrant camp who was en route to the Slovenia gap.

“Taliban good!” he told me in pidgin English when I asked his opinion about the ruling terrorist group in his home country.

A Breach in the Defenses

The Balkan routes generally run northwest from Turkey through countries like Greece, Macedonia, Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia. Migrants know that once they penetrate into the periphery of the E.U., a borderless inter-nation agreement (the Schengen Zone) enables inspection-free travel to rich and desirable interior countries like France.

A decade ago, ISIS fed its terrorist operatives into the migrant flows. They went on to kill and wound hundreds of French and Belgian citizens in 2015 and 2016, while dozens of other border-crossing migrants committed small terror attacks throughout Europe. Because of this mayhem, the E.U.’s external countries buttoned up their borders with stout fences and instant-expulsion policies backed by rigorous patrolling.

E.U. member Hungary started it off in 2015 with an electrified barbed wire double fence, which immediately choked off the main channel through Croatia and Serbia. When migrants diverted west to avoid it, Austria built another, forcing Slovenia to build a razor-wire fence along the border with Croatia to head off further spillover.

By 2016, the Balkan routes were considered effectively closed. It also helped that the E.U. paid Turkey and some proxy North African nations (and violent militias) billions of euros to stop and block emigration from their territories.

So how did another mass migration start in 2022 that would flood France with tens of thousands more?

In June 2022, Slovenian voters threw out the center-right Slovenian Democratic Party that had built that fence. They elected the center-left Freedom Movement and installed Prime Minister Robert Golob, who had campaigned to tear down Slovenia’s fence and immediately set about doing so.

News Travels Fast

Word spread that a gap in Slovenia’s Balkan route had just opened, so migrants came pouring through it. I toured the forlorn remnants of Slovenia’s fence, observing broken-down sections lying where they had been pushed down. Anyone could walk through at will. I never saw a single police officer as I crossed back and forth repeatedly on foot and by car.

Smugglers and self-directed immigrants (including many from Latin America) quickly figured out they could fly without visas into Serbia for a time, or trek on their own up from Greece and into Bosnia for the onward journey through a narrow sliver of Croatian territory to Slovenia. And there they were, inside the E.U. with no opposition, free to travel to France.

E.U. governments pleaded with Croatia to police the territory. But with no wall and a porous border, Croatia was effectively unable to oblige. Immigrants on the Bosnia side told me they planned to push for the Slovenia gap and go on to France.

On the U.N.’s Camp Lipa in northwest Bosnia, for instance, nine young men from Morocco and Algeria were hardly worried about Croatian police catching them as they prepared for the short trek across Croatia to the Slovenia border.

“No problem!!!” almost everyone shouted, laughing as they turned and disappeared into the dark forest, chanting, “Inshallah! Inshallah!”—if God wills it.

Earlier this year, Slovenians elected a conservative government that plans to rebuild the fence. But that’s too late for France.

>>> Spain’s Housing Backlash Is a Warning for America

American Slovenias

Of course, though it was the liberal Slovene government that opened the side door into the E.U., it was government policies in destination countries that lured them through. France, the U.K., and other European countries have clung to policies and processes that prevent quick deportations and, at the same time, provide the arrivals with public welfare. These are powerful lures.

In 2023, immigrants told me they knew France and other destination countries wouldn’t—or couldn’t—deport them. One France-bound Algerian I encountered in northwest Bosnia answered this way when I asked how important the low probability of deportation was to him: “It’s 90 percent important,” he immediately responded. “If you do all the trip and they catch you and deport you, it’s very, very difficult. This point is very important.”

There’s a lesson for Americans in this practically unknown aspect of French politics: the United States can easily become like France if voters elect liberal politicians who favor lenient immigration policies.

Not just that, though. To avoid becoming France, U.S. policies must include making sure that Mexico and the transit countries of Central America never become the Slovenia I saw a few years ago.

#7738. Kirkland provided $11.8M in free legal work for Trump administration

Kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, according to U.S. congressional Democrats in a statement released Thursday. (Image from Shutterstock)

Kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, according to U.S. congressional Democrats in a statement released Thursday.

Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate are increasing their scrutiny of nine major law firms’ agreements with the Trump administration last year to provide nearly $1 billion in free legal services. The agreements allowed the firms to avoid executive orders targeting their legal work, political affiliations and diversity policies.

Kirkland & Ellis performed about $4 million in pro ​bono work for the Commerce Department, as well as $2.2 million for the Defense Department, according to a statement by several Democrats in the Senate and House of Representatives.

#7737. Free Speech Under Siege in France

The median American read only two books in 2025, and 40% of us read not a single book all year. The French are more literary; they read an average of 18 books a year. They venerate authors—the more intellectual, controversial, and impenetrable the better.

But that doesn’t mean authors are beyond criticism in France. The work of Michel Houellebecq, for example, has long been controversial. In 2002, he was charged with inciting racism for calling Islam “the stupidest religion.” Mosques in Paris and Lyon joined with the World Islamic League to bring the charges against him. Paris judges found him not guilty.

In response, the head of the Mosque of Lyon said, “Islam now can be insulted freely. The permission to insult Islam has now been given.”

Well, yes. That’s how free speech works. Insulting a person, institution, or religion may be unfair, unkind, or even unwise, but in these United States at least, it is not illegal. That’s why we tolerate the views of podcast harpy Jennifer Welch and chief “Groyper” Nick Fuentes, among others.

But France, like Britain and Germany, has no First Amendment. In all three countries, people are routinely arrested for speech that in the United States would be legal.

>>> France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America

Houellebecq’s book “Submission” was published in January 2015, on the same day Islamist terrorists murdered 12 journalists and staff at the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo for having republished cartoons depicting the Muslim prophet Mohammed.

“Submission” invokes an imaginary future (2022!) where a Muslim party has won national elections and governs according to Sharia law—among other things, legalizing polygamy. The protagonist, a middle-aged man, eventually decides to convert to Islam so he can have more wives.

Houellebecq took a lot of criticism for the book but was not formally charged. He was raised as a young child in Algeria at the end of its French rule, which ended in a bloody terrorist campaign and war. That experience may have shaped his bleak view of France’s future.

Houellebecq is back under investigation by a judge, this time for comments made in 2022 in an interview with the outlet Front Populaire. The investigation was instigated by a complaint from the Grand Mosque of Paris in 2023 and may result in criminal charges.

Here’s some of what he said. (Translation by The Critic. It sounds better in French):

The wish of the native French population is not that Muslims assimilate but that they stop robbing and assaulting them. Or, another solution, that they leave. … When entire territories come under Islamist control, I think acts of resistance will take place. There will be attacks and shootings in mosques, in cafés frequented by Muslims, in short, Bataclans in reverse.

The “great replacement” theory “[is] not a theory, it’s a fact. It’s statistical evidence.”

The first two statements are his opinion. The second is unsavory, especially given the reportedly racially motivated October murder in Paris of a black French national. But it is his prediction, not an incitement to violence.

The third statement, as Houellebecq says, is fact. European populations across the West are shrinking, while foreign peoples immigrate in large numbers. One thus replaces the other. We can discuss whether this is good or bad, or why it happens, but not the undeniable fact that it is occurring.

But whether he is right or wrong is not the issue. The protesters taking to the streets every week in France are motivated by various causes from teacher shortages to pensions to Gaza, not an interview in Front Populaire they never read. I doubt any of the young men in Marseille looting luxury stores for sneakers and bags have read a book, let alone one by Michel Houellebecq.

>>> The Unexpected Source of Muslim Immigration to France

In a recent interview with Ben Shapiro, comedian and writer Rob Schneider said:

When the truth becomes a right-wing concept, then I think you have to stand up for it…It’s going to cost you to speak your opinion. It’s going to cost you jobs, it’s going to cost you money, but it’s going to cost you more if you don’t speak up and you lose this incredible experiment in freedom that we have.

America was founded on free speech, which is the only way to get to the truth. If we lose that, we lose all. France’s revolution followed ours by 13 years. But whereas ours was against an occupying overseas power, theirs was internal and devolved into a purge for ideological purity. Free speech was the very basis of our revolution, but it was an early casualty in theirs.

I was U.S. Consul in Slovakia for three years. Everyone my age there remembered life under communism. The system survived partly because of the Soviet Union’s threat of military force, which they used in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968 to suppress popular uprisings. But Czechoslovakia and the other Soviet satellite states also had repressive police, informers, and political prisons to keep people down.

People shared bitter jokes, such as “we pretend to work, and they pretend to pay us,” about socialist economics. They listened to jazz, which was subversive without words. They listened to Voice of America and read books in secret. But they knew better than to speak out freely against the communist system unless they were prepared for the gulag or death. That’s why it lasted almost 50 years.

If convicted, Houellebecq could face up to a year in prison and heavy fines. But behind bars with him would go France’s freedom of speech. We watch from America as our oldest ally—along with Britain, Germany, and others—goes down this well-worn path to authoritarian censorship. Whatever happens there, we need to hold fast to our principles here:

“Congress shall make no law…abridging the freedom of speech…”

#7736. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7735. The Wages of War

Consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.

The Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.

Since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.

Virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.

>>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock

Since energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.

For example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.

But the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.

All that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.

Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.

But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.

>>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only Temporary

That’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.

That’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.

It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.

Unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.

To be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

#7734. Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The ruling on Section 287(g) agreements overturns an earlier district court decision.

In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's new law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) issue:

We vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:

We conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

The anti-mask law presents more difficult issues because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:

At bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law.  Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

#7733. New Jersey’s “Islamophobia” Bill Is a Blasphemy Law in Disguise

New Jersey legislators are considering a bill that would be the first in the nation to define “Islamophobia.” It’s not merely descriptive, however. It is so overbroad that it would make it all but impossible to evaluate Islam and the culture it produces in any meaningful way.

That is because a provision in it mandates that public officials and law enforcement officers use the bill’s definitions when considering whether a civil or criminal law has been violated.

It is sure to run into American protections for free speech that are unusually strong even by Western standards. Adherents of every religion have learned over the centuries that hearing their faith smeared, even irrationally (Islamophobia means “an irrational fear of Islam”), is a price they want to pay.

The bill comes as the election of several Muslims to political office nationwide has refocused attention on the nature of Islam and especially its political dimension, or Islamism.

Television scenes of Muslim youth ransacking stores, government offices, and national symbols in France and throughout Europe have also drawn attention to the capacity, or even willingness, of Western societies to assimilate immigrants from the Muslim world. A political alliance between Islamism and the Left is another factor often discussed.

The New Jersey bill, A1146, is moreover championed by the Council on American-Islamic Relations, a pressure group devoted to increasing the number of Muslim elected officials, but which has been declared a “foreign terrorist organization” in Texas and Florida because of its association with the Muslim Brotherhood.

>>> Free Speech Under Siege in France

All of this puts A1146 in the crossroads of a volatile debate growing in America and around the world—a debate which A1146 seems expressly made to shut down.

The clause at the very end of the bill requiring that the definitions be used in investigations makes clear that what is at hand is not merely an exercise in informing the citizenry about what constitutes Islamophobia (already a loaded term). It says in full that:

In reviewing, investigating, or deciding whether there has been a violation of any policy, law, or regulation prohibiting discriminatory acts under the civil or criminal laws of this State, a public official or law enforcement officer shall take into consideration the definition of Islamophobia contained in subsection a. of this section for the purposes of determining whether the alleged act was motivated by Islamophobia and discriminatory anti-Muslim intent.

Subsection A has 13 different definitions that would catch in its nettle now viewed as legitimate. It starts by asserting that Islamophobia includes “hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture.”

The second would also chill debate, saying that Islamophobia includes “hostility and fear of Islam, and as a result, a fear of and aversion to all Muslims or the majority of Muslims.”

Same for No. 5, which includes “making mendacious, dehumanizing, demonizing, or stereotypical allegations about Muslims, or of Muslims as a collective group.”

No. 11 carries no small degree of irony with regard to the Garden State. It stipulates that Islamophobia includes “accusing Muslim citizens of being more loyal to a transnational Muslim community or to their countries of origin, or to the alleged priorities of Muslims worldwide, than to the interests of the people of New Jersey or the interests of the people of the United States.”

But it just so happens that Adam Hamawy, an observant Muslim just elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in New Jersey’s 12th District, was repeatedly asked on CNN’s Situation Room whether he views Iran, a country we’re at war with, as an adversary—and he declined to do so.

The Heritage report makes another important point when it observes that “Western European countries, including the United Kingdom and France, are now experiencing recurring conflicts tantamount to a national identity crisis related to large, unassimilated Muslim populations.”

The All-Party Parliamentary Group’s 2018 report defining Islamophobia was adopted by several political parties and institutions, despite its potential infringement on free speech.

The APPG report was strongly influenced by the Muslim Council of Britain—which, according to another of the papers we published last week, was established and is run by the Muslim Brotherhood.

The Brotherhood, writes French anthropologist Florence Bergeaud-Blackler in that other paper, “has engaged in a century-old project to ‘Islamify modernity’ through gradual, lawful, multisector action” and it is doing so “across Europe, and now across the United States.”
