#7732. AFT Boss Randi Weingarten’s Sleazy Book Scam Keeps Growing—and Teachers Paid for It All

Becoming a teacher is no way to get rich, but becoming the head of a teachers union? That’s a different story.

Take Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, who received $546,158 in total compensation last year, according to the union’s latest financial disclosure.

That’s over seven times the $74,495 average salary earned by public-school teachers nationwide.

And the new documents, recently filed with the federal Labor Department, show that an AFT president’s cronies can profit handsomely, too.

Outside consultants, a New York law firm, a public-relations firm and others appear to have raked in more than $2.2 million from AFT coffers to help Weingarten produce her 2025 book “Why Fascists Fear Teachers”—up from the more than $1.4 million previously estimated by the Freedom Foundation and reported by The Post.

The payments break down across two filings, covering two separate fiscal years.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Dirty Back-to-School War on Target

The first, for a one-year period from 2024 to 2025, documented substantial costs connected to the book paid by the AFT—including payments to Weingarten’s literary agent Inkwell Management, to a fact-checker credited in her acknowledgments, and to a photographer for her author’s headshot.

The new form adds further amounts apparently related to the same project.

On Sept. 25, 2025, nine days after the book’s release, the AFT paid Inkwell Management $28,125 for a “publication expense,” bringing combined payments to the agent across both filings to $92,215.

Separately, the union paid Feldman Strategies, a publicity firm, $202,500; shortly after the pub date, the PR group posted, “It has been a true honor for our entire team at Feldman Strategies to help promote” Weingarten’s book.

The new filing also records an $80,000 “royalty payment” sent on Oct. 23, 2025, to a limited liability company controlled by Weingarten.

That sum follows a $125,000 royalty payment to the same entity disclosed in the union’s prior annual report, bringing the combined royalty transfers from AFT to the Weingarten-controlled company to $205,000.

And in its 2026 filing, the union paid Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler LLP — the law firm credited in the book with reviewing Weingarten’s manuscript—another $591,174, bringing cumulative legal fees to the firm across both years to nearly $1.6 million.

The union says the firm toiled on the book “pro bono,” but the attorneys’ extensive financial ties to the AFT create an obvious incentive to characterize that work as such.

The royalty payments require additional explanation: Public filings show the AFT itself receiving publisher advances connected to the book, then disbursing a portion of those funds as a “royalty payment” to Teachers Want What Kids Need, LLC—an entity controlled by Weingarten.

The publisher did not pay royalties to Weingarten or her LLC directly; the money flowed through the union, in an arrangement that remains opaque.

Weingarten has stated that some of the book’s proceeds would go back to the AFT, the AFT Disaster Relief Fund, and the AFT Educational Foundation.

Even if that claim holds, dues-paying teachers shouldn’t be required to subsidize a book project that profits their union’s president.

In July, the GOP-led House Committee on Education and the Workforce opened a formal inquiry into the matter based on The Post’s initial report, requesting documents on the AFT’s book-related expenditures, contracts and royalty flows.

That inquiry is controlled by the committee majority, however—and once Democrats take control of the House in January, the probe is expected to stall or be closed.

The minority can still request materials and issue reports, but it cannot compel the same level of investigation.

Separately, the Department of Labor’s Inspector General has already opened its own review to probe whether union dues were improperly used for Weingarten’s book project.

That executive-branch inquiry can continue under President Donald Trump’s administration, regardless of which party controls Congress.

>>> Randi Weingarten’s Convention Exposes the Teachers’ Union as a Political Machine

The new 2026 filing supplies further evidence that any ongoing review should examine: The additional royalty payment, the fresh publication expense routed to the literary agent, the large PR contract and the further $591,174 to Patterson Belknap all post-date the period covered by the prior report.

Payments to the Weingarten-controlled entity, the literary agent, the PR firm and the consultants raise questions about whether dues money collected from teachers was used for the personal benefit of the union’s top officer.

Federal labor filings exist precisely so that members and the public can review such expenditures.

When these records show repeated transfers linked to an officer’s private project, the disclosures themselves supply the basis for scrutiny.

Teachers who don’t want their hard-earned paychecks to underwrite an officer’s vanity project have a practical alternative.

Organizations such as the Teacher Freedom Alliance offer membership—including free liability insurance—without routing teacher dues to electoral campaigns or left-wing causes.

If enough fed-up teachers leave the AFT, people like Randi Weingarten might think twice about wasting members’ money on personal and political pet projects.

#7730. Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The federal law did not prohibit the basic AR-15 rifle design.

Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004.  The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today."

That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v).  So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated.  The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof.  Second, they included certain features, including:

a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –

(ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;

(iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and

(v) a grenade launcher….  18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

Under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names.  A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

But guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip.  None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design.  Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock.  How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount?  A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could.  Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

And so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design.  Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

Manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance.  I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw).  As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

Connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994.  The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design.  And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

NEXT: Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

Stephen Halbrook is a Senior Fellow with the Independent Institute. His latest books are America's Rifle: The Case for the AR-15 and The Right to Bear Arms: A Constitutional Right of the People or a Privilege of the Ruling Class? He is also author of The Founders' Second Amendment, Securing Civil Rights, Gun Control in the Third Reich, and Gun Control in Nazi-Occupied France. He has written over 30 law review articles and has testified in Congressional hearings on firearm law bills. He has also litigated extensively in the field, often representing groups such as the NRA, National African American Gun Association, Western States Sheriffs' Association, Congress of Racial Equality, National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, and more. He has argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in Castillo v. U.S. (2000), Printz v. U.S. (1997), and U.S. v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. (1992), as well as in front of many other courts.  In D.C. v. Heller, he filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of a majority of members of Congress.

The Fourth District Court of Appeal in Florida on Wednesday banned a disbarred Florida attorney convicted of fraud from submitting pro se filings in his case after he allegedly “flooded” a trial court with documents, many generated with artificial intelligence.

#7728. Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums. His meticulously planned heists are executed with a showman’s flair. The anti-hero of the hit Netflix series Lupin, portrayed to perfection by actor Omar Sy, Diop dons elaborate disguises, slips into fake identities, and turns on the charm as he swipes priceless gems and outwits the police.

He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc. Lupin made his debut in 1905, at the height of the glamorous Belle Époque, and was featured in two dozen novels and short story collections. A skilled burglar and a master of disguise, this impish shapeshifter relishes the challenge of stealing the un-stealable and often returns the treasures he pilfers. He’s more interested in righting wrongs than living off ill-gotten gains. So is Diop – he’s determined to exonerate his father, who was wrongly accused of stealing a priceless necklace from the powerful and corrupt businessman Hubert Pellegrini.

Diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023. As Lupin returns for a long-anticipated fourth season, here’s a lineup of five of the slickest gentlemen thieves of fiction:

A.J. Raffles: Lupin was France’s answer to a wildly popular English thief of fiction. In 1898, E. W. Hornung (the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle) published the first of twenty-six stories on the adventures of Arthur Raffles, a London man-about-town and star cricket player who steals to support his expensive lifestyle and keep up appearances. His speciality is cracking safes and he enlists a sidekick from his school days, Bunny Manders, as a partner-in-crime.

Despite his crooked side-gig, Raffles adheres to a gentlemanly moral code. He shudders at the thought of preying on a host or a friend, and rarely packs a gun when he sets out to steal. “It would be very awkward if anything went wrong,” he tells Manders. “One might use it, and that’s not the game at all.” He stalks the corrupt and the obscenely wealthy, reasoning that “the immorally rich” are the logical targets for a “richly immoral” thief like himself.

Hercule Flambeau: His name may sound like that of a certain Belgian detective, but Flambeau’s obsession is stealing jewels, not solving crimes. That changes after a run-in with a priest and part-time detective dreamed up by writer G.K. Chesterton. In the first Father Brown short story, “The Blue Cross,” published in 1910, the clergyman with a kindly demeanor and a keen sense of human nature foils Flambeau’s attempt to steal a religious relic.

Like Lupin, Flambeau is one of France’s most-wanted criminals – Chesterton described him as a “colossus of crime” with a long record of “ingenious and wholesale robbery.” And like Lupin, he can disguise himself and hide in plain sight, despite being over six feet tall. He is also “a startling acrobat,” wrote his creator, who “could leap like a grasshopper and melt into the tree-tops like a monkey.” Flambeau became a recurring character, appearing in more than a dozen of the fifty-three Father Brown stories, and not only reforms but eventually helps the clergyman to crack cases.

John Robie: It’s the early 1950s on the French Riviera and Robie, a wily burglar whose agility earned him the nickname “Le Chat” before he was caught and imprisoned, is forced out of retirement when a copycat makes him a suspect in new crimes. The protagonist in American travel writer David Dodge’s 1952 novel To Catch a Thief sets out to trap his doppelgänger.

Robie is the consummate gentleman thief – dashing, clever, a master of his calling. Who better to portray him when Alfred Hitchcock brought the story to the big screen in 1955 than the king of suave, Cary Grant. “For what it’s worth,” Grant-as-Robie points out in a line added for the movie, “I never stole from anybody who would go hungry.”

Sir Charles Lytton: Peter Sellers’s hilariously inept Inspector Jacques Clouseau debuted in the 1963 movie The Pink Panther, but the real star of the blockbuster franchise’s first instalment was David Niven. He was cast as the debonaire playboy Sir Charles Lytton, who leads a double life as an elusive jewel thief known as “The Phantom.” Niven was an inspired choice – he played Raffles on screen in 1939, in one of many films to feature Hornung’s character.

The Pink Panther is reputed to be the world’s largest diamond and Lytton has come to a ski resort in the Italian Alps to steal it. The bumbling Clouseau is there to try to stop him. Niven may have enjoyed top billing as a classy crook but Sellers’s over-the-top performance stole the show and hijacked the franchise.

Danny Ocean: Frank Sinatra was the first to tackle the role of the ringleader of a gang of thieves who rob five Las Vegas casinos on New Year’s Eve in the 1960 movie Ocean’s 11. George Clooney revived the character four decades later in 2001’s Ocean’s Eleven, with Danny assembling a team of skilled crooks (an all-star cast that includes Brad Pitt and Matt Damon) to loot a supposedly impregnable Vegas vault.

The movie inspired two sequels, with the gang reuniting to steal a Fabergé egg in Ocean’s Twelve and a casino’s cash and a trove of diamonds in Ocean’s Thirteen. In each movie the targets are fellow thieves or ruthless, unscrupulous moguls. The heists are filled with Lupin-worthy disguises and deceptions and Clooney is a natural for the modern iteration of the cool, classy crook.

It’s little wonder the gentleman thief is a staple of fiction. His victims are fellow travellers who deserve to be cut down to size, or have insurance policies or pockets deep enough to absorb their losses. Admiring their audacity and cheering them on is a guilty pleasure we can all enjoy.

Dean Jobb’s latest true crime book, A Gentleman and a Thief: The Daring Jewel Heists of a Jazz Age Rogue (Algonquin Books and HarperCollins Canada), is a New York Times Editors’ Choice and a national bestseller in Canada. It’s the story of Arthur Barry, who charmed the elite of 1920s New York City while planning and executing some of the most brazen jewel thefts in history. Find him at deanjobb.com.

#7727. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7726. Second Amendment Roundup, II: Much Ado About Bowie Knives

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Laws on concealed carry are not historical analogues for banning semiautomatic rifles.

In Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment.  If Bowie knives in common use by law-abiding citizens may be banned, the argument goes, so too may semiautomatic rifles.

A word of caution.  To paraphrase Freud, sometimes a knife is just a knife.  Knives generally have a point and an edge on one side, sometimes also an edge on the other.  Any knife can be used for good or bad.  Bruen distinguished heavy weapons of war like lancegays from daggers, noting that in medieval society "[a]lmost everyone carried a knife or a dagger in his belt," "[c]ivilians wore them for self-protection," and "the smaller medieval weapons … strike us as most analogous to modern handguns."

No doubt Bowie knives were in use as tools for skinning game and self-defense, and ruffians are said to have carried them concealed.  But for a variety of reasons, it's unnecessary to decide whether Bowie knives met the Heller test of being in common use.  Four of the amicus briefs are right on point on this issue: National Rifle Ass'n (NRA), National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF), Senator Ted Cruz, and the United States (U.S.).

First, a few States' restrictions are not enough to establish a historical tradition.  Under Heller, a handful of outlier laws cannot justify a ban.  "Most States regulated Bowie knives in some manner, but, except in a few outlier jurisdictions, adults were free to buy, possess, and openly carry them. Regulations typically restricted concealed carry, sales to minors, or imposed enhanced penalties for criminal misuse." NRA Br. 5.

Second, "No State banned Bowie-knife possession in the nineteenth century." NRA Br. 36.  "And one of the only laws that likely did actually ban Bowie knives (along with pistols and an array of other items) is the same 1837 Georgia law that was promptly held unconstitutional other than as applied to concealed carry—because it was too restrictive to comply with the Second Amendment. See 1837 Ga. Acts 90, §1 (1838); Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243 (1846); cf. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 54 (singling out Nunn as "particularly instructive" on the Second Amendment's meaning)." NSSF Br. 21.

These were concealed-carry restrictions, not complete bans.  "This Court has already concluded that restrictions on concealed carry cannot justify carry bans, see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 48-49, 53-55, let alone possession bans, see Heller, 554 U.S. at 628-29." NSSF Br. 21.

Third, the same laws covered handguns.  "If those laws justified rifle bans, then handgun bans would be justified all the more, because they typically also regulated handguns but not long guns." NRA Br. 38.

Where Bowie-knife restrictions were upheld, courts applied the same standard Petitioners advance here: arms in common use for lawful purposes are protected, while weapons used only by criminals are not.  As Judge Richardson's dissent in Bianchi explains, it does not matter that courts sometimes disagreed about whether Bowie knives were in fact in common use, because they were applying the same yardstick. "State courts have long applied the common-use test to judge such laws under state constitutional provisions securing the right to bear arms." U.S. Br. 12.

Fourth, even a court that viewed the Bowie knife as exceptionally deadly held that the right to carry it was protected.  "And Texas's Cockrum v. State held a Bowie knife to be a protected arm—"[t]he right to carry a bowie-knife for lawful defense is secured, and must be admitted"— while sustaining an enhanced penalty for its abuse, treating the weapon's dangerousness as a reason to regulate its misuse, not a reason to deny that it was an arm. 24 Tex. 394, 402-403 (1859).  Cockrum is the mirror image of the decision below: alleged dangerousness bore on regulation, not on coverage." Cruz Br. 18.

The historical answer to misuse was punishing criminals, not disarming law-abiding citizens

"[T]he evil must be prevented by the penitentiary and gallows, and not by a general deprivation of a constitutional privilege." U.S. Br. 30 (quoting Wilson v. State).

Stephen Halbrook is a Senior Fellow with the Independent Institute. His latest books are America's Rifle: The Case for the AR-15 and The Right to Bear Arms: A Constitutional Right of the People or a Privilege of the Ruling Class? He is also author of The Founders' Second Amendment, Securing Civil Rights, Gun Control in the Third Reich, and Gun Control in Nazi-Occupied France. He has written over 30 law review articles and has testified in Congressional hearings on firearm law bills. He has also litigated extensively in the field, often representing groups such as the NRA, National African American Gun Association, Western States Sheriffs' Association, Congress of Racial Equality, National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, and more. He has argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in Castillo v. U.S. (2000), Printz v. U.S. (1997), and U.S. v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. (1992), as well as in front of many other courts.  In D.C. v. Heller, he filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of a majority of members of Congress.

#7725. The top five Watsons (read: “often impressed best friend narrators”) in crime fiction

I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally. By “Watson,” I refer to the archetype of the Very Impressed Best Friend And Narrator. A hype man who also tells the story. A deputy who keeps going “wow, look at this guy” as he tells you about this guy. Bonus points if he’s also this guy’s roommate.

That’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series. He’s a carnival barker and a nonfiction writer. Sherlock Holmes is not only his friend, he’s also his subject. Watson isn’t only HIS best friend, he’s also his audience. But he’s also his publicist. He‘s fascinated by Holmes, and he knows tons of people will also be fascinated by Holmes. His job is PR, and man does he do it well.

Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.

Watson: Archie Goodwin  Detective: Nero Wolfe

In the beloved Rex Stout series, the young Archie Goodwin narrates AND does all the legwork for the affluent, grouchy, high-on-the-horse bibliophile and private detective Nero Wolfe (who hates leaving his luxurious brownstone). Archie, a handsome and dapper young man, is a quick-witted, fast-talking factotum. And he’s always pretty impressed with the mental calculations of his sedentary boss.

Watson: S.S. Van Dine Detective: Philo Vance

S.S. Van Dine takes the Watson gambit even further than Watson does. S.S. Van Dine is a real person, the real-life writer of the Philo Vance books (though “S.S. Van Dine” was a pen name; his real name was Willard Huntington Wright), who writes himself into the stories as the best friend of the brilliant, suave, dandyish detective Philo Vance. Here, he’s not Vance’s creator, merely his chronicler, and the two solve innumerable mysteries together during the Jazz Age.

Watson: Unnamed  Detective: C. Auguste Dupin

We don’t know the name of the guy who narrates his friend and roommate Auguste Dupin’s feats of investigation, but he is really the OG Watson. They meet at various rare booksellers and eventually hit it off, becoming pals and then deciding to move in together. And then the unnamed narrator marvels as Dupin solves crimes, sometimes after hitting the scene of the crime, sometimes without leaving their house.

Watson: Capt. Arthur Hastings  Detective: Hercule Poirot

Hercule Poirot’s best friend Arthur Hastings doesn’t narrate ALL the Poirot stories (he narrates eight of thirty-three novels, and twenty-one of fifty-one short stories), because, after Hastings meets a beautiful music hall performer half his age in Murder on the Links, he marries her and eventually moves with her to South America, where they have four kids. But Hastings still appears, sprinkled throughout the Poirot canon, because he returns to England for business a lot. So they get together and crime-solve then.

Watson: Anthony Horowitz Detective: Daniel Hawthorne

Look, I’d have such a soft spot for Anthony Horowitz even WITHOUT the these books, simply because I grew up reading the Alex Rider series. But the Horowitz and Hawthorne mysteries, in which “Horowitz himself” tags along as the sidekick and narrator (he’s NOT ONLY the Watson, here, but also the Van Dine), are so delightful. I love these guys. Their work is very collaborative (and these books are sneaky, since Hawthorne isn’t the real mastermind, but Horowitz himself). And often, they’re at odds. But that’s fine. This subgenre loves nuance. Horowitz is a Watson with his own (even more impressive) list of mystery bona-fides than his subject, which is what makes this series even more interesting.

#7724. Bob Woodward Interviews Justice Kagan, Or Does Justice Kagan Interview Bob Woodward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Kagan sheds some light on her view about leaks, Dobbs, and the Court.

Last month I wrote about an excerpt from Bob Woodward's new book that reveals sources. Most of the sources are deceased, so there is little harm outing them. But Justices Kagan and Breyer are alive and well. Woodward reveals a remarkable conversation with the former. As Woodward would observe, it is less clear that he was interviewing Kagan than Kagan was interviewing him.

"Well, the conclusion of The Brethren was that the center of the court was in control," I said, meaning neither the left nor the right was in charge. "Yes, I prefer it that way," Kagan said. "That's exactly what it should be." That's not the way it is now, I noted. It is not, Kagan confirmed. How did you get such detail in the book? We had time, I said. Of course, it was a different era in which Scott and I were doing the reporting in the late 1970s. I started to tell her about Scott and how he had really discovered the Nixon Tapes because he found Alexander Butterfield. Not letting me off the hook, Kagan asked again, "How did you do it?" Well, we interviewed five sitting justices and 170 law clerks. We got documentation. That's extraordinary, Kagan said. How did you get the documents? The justices must have approved the clerks giving you the documents? I shook my head. Not that we were aware. You make clerks now sign nondisclosure agreements, I noted. "Yes," she said.

Over the years, I've speculated that Justices have authorized their clerks to leak information to the press. The premise of Kagan's questions is that Justices had authorized their clerks to speak with Woodward and Bernstein. But no, the clerks went rogue. If the clerks acted alone in the 1970s, perhaps they did so in 2022 with the Dobbs opinion.

I told her that Brennan and Marshall, the liberal justices on the court, would not help us. Well, who did? Rehnquist and White, I said. Kagan seemed surprised. I recounted the story of calling Justice Lewis Powell at the court one morning and him agreeing to meet. I said when and he said now. "I was in my pajamas, but told him I'd be there in half an hour." You must be fast, Kagan said. I was then, I joked. I was 79 now and slow.

Justice Kagan clerked for Justice Marshall, who apparently never discussed the sourcing for The Brethren.

Is all of this known about The Brethren? Kagan asked. I didn't have an answer so instead I dived into Blackmun's role in Roe v. Wade and how he had drafted the opinion at the Mayo Clinic library. "I thought the leak of the Dobbs decision was a public service," I told her, referencing the decision that had overturned Roe the previous year. I can't say I agree with that, Kagan said. Why do you think it's a public service? Well, the court took away a right that had been there for 50 years. The public needed to know so there could be a debate. Kagan didn't say anything.

I find it odd that Kagan said nothing in response. This is not the sort of statement that could trigger a recusal. She might have said "that debate nearly got my colleague assassinated." But she stayed silent.

I said from reporting more than 50 years on 10 presidents, I thought there was such a concentration of power in the presidency. Too much power.

She nodded. It's why Trump was able to get away with so much, I said. Kagan did not respond. Then I said, there's too much power in the Supreme Court maybe. She noticeably reacted to that, her head held a little higher, her posture stiffening. Her only reply was, "That's interesting."

She mustered a response here, but not to the leak question. Interesting?

"Are you happy on the court?" I asked her. No, I'm not, given the situation, Kagan replied. I was surprised at her candor.

Kagan likely didn't think she would be quoted.

As we parted ways, she smiled warmly and said she respected my work and I said I respected hers. Late that night I recorded a detailed voice memo of my conversation with Kagan for my assistant to transcribe. It is hard to tell who was interviewing who.

On Saturday, October 21, 2023, Elsa and I attended a dinner for the 50th anniversary of the Saturday Night Massacre hosted by the former Watergate special prosecutors at the WilmerHale law firm in downtown Washington. The main speaker was retired Supreme Court justice Stephen Breyer, who had been a junior Watergate prosecutor. Elsa sat next to Breyer at the dinner before switching seats with me. He had served 28 years on the Supreme Court and told her he was "forced out" so someone younger could take his place.

No one forced him out. He has life tenure. Instead, Breyer surrendered to the pressure. So much for judicial independence. Justices Alito and Thomas are often charged with being MAGA partisans, but they exhibited robust independence from political forces.

Woodward offers this anecdote about the Thomas confirmation hearing:

Later Gray told me it took five years for Clarence Thomas to recover. Justice Thomas's wife, Ginni Thomas, a conservative activist, approached me at a conference in Washington one day. She said after the hearings her husband was never really a whole person again. He hardened. Many conservatives, including attorney general for George H. W. Bush and for Donald Trump, Bill Barr, have said the hearings pushed Thomas to the hard right.

I couldn't find any references to other current justices.

I will read the chapters on The Brethren with interest.

#7723. Setting the Record Straight On Senator Cornyn And The N.D. Tex. Seat (Updated)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

At the outset of President Trump's second term, there were a number of vacant district court seats throughout Texas. A reasonable person might have predicted that given two Republican senators, those seats would be filled quickly, but no such luck. The first nomination--Nicholas Ganjei for S.D.Tex--was not made until November 2025. Yes, while Missouri quickly filled all the seats, Texas lagged behind. Two more nominations in the Western District were made in January 2026--Andrew Davis for the Austin seat and Chis Wolfe for the Waco seat. It's worth noting that both Ganjei and Davis served as Chief Counsel for Senator Cruz. And the story of the Waco seat is enough for another post. In April 2026, two more nominations were made for S.D. Tex. seats in the Valley: John Marck and Arthur Jones.

Up to this point, none of the vacancies in the Northern District of Texas were tapped. Finally, in May 2026, Kasdin Mitchell was nominated to one of the seats in N.D. Tex. At that time, Angela Colmenero was tapped for another seat in Houston. Four more months would lapse. In September, Richard Bennett was nominated for a seat in Houston and Courtney Coker was nominated for a seat in Dallas.

But there were still two open seats. The critical vacancy was the Western District of Texas seat in Austin, which had remained open for some time. Virtually all of the litigation against the state government is filed in Austin. And, for reasons that continue to elude me, David Ezra, a senior judge from Hawaii, brings the Aloha Spirit to muck up Texas jurisprudence.

Shortly after the midterm election, President Trump nominated Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court for the Austin seat. Around the same time, Trump nominated Elliot Gaiser for the remaining N.D. Tex. in Dallas. Ultimately, Senator Cornyn would block Gaiser's nomination, and urged the White House to nominate Steve Fahey. That's where thing stand now.

Many people, even those in Texas, cannot make sense of this situation. Why on earth did it take so long to fill all of these seats? Why did nominations for the final two seats only come after the election? Why did Trump pick Gaiser if Cornyn had objections?

Let me try to set the record straight on a few matters here.

Traditionally, Texas District court nominees have gone through something called the Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee (FJEC). Senators Cornyn and Cruz have used this structure to allow local attorneys (now about 30) to make recommendations on potential judicial candidates. The committee will screen applications, conduct interview, and recommend finalists to the Senators. Generally, if both senators sign off on a finalist, they recommend the name to the White House. At that point, the White House will conduct an interview, and if things work out, a nomination is made. I hedge slightly, because sometimes the process goes in a different order. It can happen that the White House really likes a particular candidate, and speaks to them in parallel, or even before the FJEC process goes through. But FJEC remains a central cog in any district court nomination.

For more than a year, there has been something of a standoff concerning the N.D. Tex. seat. There were two relevant finalists from FJEC. The first was Michael Berry, a Marine Veteran, longtime attorney with the First Liberty Institute, and--perhaps most importantly--former Chief Counsel to Senator Cruz. The second was Steve Fahey, a lawyer I did not know. He was an assistant United States Attorney until 2021, and now has a solo private practice. I'm told one of his most significant case was seeking a writ of coram nobis to protect an illegal alien from deportation. (The petition was denied.)

Senator Cornyn blocked Berry. Or to be more precise, Cornyn's Chief Counsel, Franci Becker, blocked Berry. The exact reason is not entirely clear. I've heard some rumors that Becker blames Berry for blocking another district court nominee, but that never happened. Senator Cruz supported that nominee. The White House found problems in that nom's record that would have made confirmation impossible. Ultimately, she withdrew from the search, and took a lucrative in-house position. Another explanation is that Becker, and Cornyn, opposed Berry because he was too conservative. Whatever the reasons, Berry had deep ties to Texas. The White House had interviewed Berry, and was prepared to make the nomination, but Cornyn kept saying no. The Washington Examiner reports on this story.

What about Fahey? I'm told that Cruz never actually blocked Fahey, but the White House had reservations about the nominee--especially his work defending illegal aliens. Ultimately, the decision was made to just let the seat stay open and it would be filled once Cornyn is out of office. The Austin seat was vital, as it involves so much state-wide litigation, but the Dallas division seats are interchangeable. This is not Amarillo or Wichita Falls. Indeed, even if Paxton were to lose the election, the Senate was likely to stay in Republican control, and a deal could be made with Senator Talarico for the Dallas seat. Alas, the election day bloodbath changed things.

The Sullivan nomination for the Austin seat was made quite quickly, even though it had been in the works for a while. Sullivan had already gone through the background check, as well as the FJEC approval. But what about Elliot Gaiser? It is true that Gaiser did not go through FJEC, but he had something very important: a recent FBI background check and Senate confirmation. He could (in theory) be slotted into the final confirmation hearing planned for November 18.

Despite my best efforts, Senator Cornyn blocked Gaiser's nomination. Cornyn (or at least someone on his staff) put out this social media post to explain his actions:

If President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience, and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide "advise and consent," which is impossible without consultation.

Still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel. All that is needed is an FBI background check with they stand ready to do on a timely basis.

Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence.

This post is misleading. Why did Trump wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The short answer is that Cornyn blocked the White House's and Cruz's preferred candidate, and the White House did not want to pick Cornyn's candidate. That's how things work. Senators can withhold consent by not returning a blue slip. But they can't force the White House to make a nomination they don't wish to make. The White House then tried a list-ditch effort to get someone into the seat before the new Congress concluded. I'm sure the administration was hoping that Senator Cornyn would realize that a filled seat is better than an empty seat, but he refused, and blocked Gaiser. Moreover, Cornyn refused to even meet with Gaiser, so he is no position to complain about a "lack of consultation." FJEC could have performed a review of Gaiser on short notice, but it was never convened.

Cornyn says Fahey was "was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee." But that does not mean Senator Cruz himself approved of Fahey. Indeed, Senator Cruz can still withhold a blue slip of Fahey. That comeuppance would be just, after Cornyn blocked both Berry and Gaiser unreasonably. Cornyn has earned no favors at this point--especially after cursing at Cruz on the Senate floor and calling him a "fragile thing" on social media. After the events of the past few weeks, I think James Talarico would be a more trustworthy partner on nominees than Cornyn. Remember, Cornyn aided and abetted the spiking of Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the Eighth Circuit. Soon enough, Judge Ada Brown's NDTX seat will become open--either through resignation or impeachment. I can see a deal being made with Cruz gets one of the Dallas seats and Talarico gets the other. All Cornyn could do that point is grouse.

The bigger problem is that there is no time left for a hearing. The November 18 hearing was the end of the show. Cornyn's stunt is now putting pressure on Senator Grassley to break even more China by holding a December nomination hearing. There is no reason that Grassley should give Cornyn this courtesy--especially after the recent stunts Cornyn has pulled.

This post is based on my best understanding of some complex deliberations over the course of nearly two years. If you spot any errors, please send me an email.

Update: Tuesday evening, the press secretary from Senator Cornyn's post reached out and said "It's inaccurate to say that Franci Becker is responsible for blocking Mike Berry's nomination." She asked me to post a statement, which I will do:

Attributable to a Cornyn spokesperson, Franci Becker did not block Mike Berry's nomination, as staff in Senate offices do not have the authority to make decisions about a nominee, and the claims in this story were not corroborated by Sen. Cornyn's office.

Of course, the ultimate decision to sign a blue slip belongs to the Senator. In any office, a staffer cannot take a final action. So in a hyper-technical sense, no staffer is capable of blocking any nominee. But Chief Counsels routinely make decisions about candidates that their senators defer to.

What the statement does not say is far more important than what it actually says. There is no denial along the lines of, "Franci Becker played no role in Mike Berry not receiving a blue slip." I also posed a few other questions about Becker's involvement with the Dallas seat, that the press secretary did not answer.

I stand by what I wrote, which is something I have heard from multiple sources in the Senate over the course of nearly a year. Staffers from other Senator's offices thanked me for this post. Two federal judges who are familiar with the situation thanked me for writing this. People I trust and who are familiar with the situation reviewed it and found no errors.

#7722. More people use AI in court filings, new research from Stanford shows

New research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits. (Photo by Userba011d64_201/Getty Images)

New research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

According to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use. The researchers noted that this doesn’t include debt collection cases.

Among other findings, Stanford’s researchers noted that pro se litigants had higher AI adoption rates. In Santa Clara County, the share of self-represented complaints that showed signs of AI use increased from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. Meanwhile, the share of attorney-filed complaints increased from 5% to 34% during this period.

Researchers also found that the use of AI varies by case type, with employment and business complaints in California showing the highest rates. They said AI use also varies throughout court filings, with more appearances in the statement of facts and causes of actions sections.

“The sharp rise we document here corroborates that AI in the law is a question of how, not whether,” Stanford’s researchers wrote in the report.

#7721. Sara Paretsky on inventing languages and feeling kinship with older characters

For more than four decades, V.I. Warshawski, the fictional private investigator created by Sara Paretsky, has aged slowly. In her late twenties and early thirties in the first novels, Warshawski is now about fifty years old. Unfortunately for Paretsky and the rest of us, time has flown by at a normal pace. In her mid-thirties when she published her first novel, Indemnity Only, in 1982, Paretsky is now seventy-nine and has less in common with her more youthful character.

Paretsky’s newest book, Bad Company, introduces a protagonist more in line with her age: Lily Sedaka, a former CIA field agent now in her seventies. The book marks her twenty-fifth novel and the first non-Warshawski novel since Ghost Country in 1998.

Paretsky will continue writing novels about Warshawski, but this new character will enable the author to tap into her own lived experiences—complete with the aches and pains that come with age.

Like her Warshawski novels, Bad Company takes place in Chicago but with an added worldview. Sections are set in the fictional Central Asian country of Hayalistan, where Sedaka once was stationed. In an interview conducted over Zoom, Paretsky reflected on the decision to introduce a new character and the difficulty that came with inventing a language.

L. Wayne Hicks: I wanted to ask you what made you decide to unveil a new character after so much success with the V.I. Warshawski novels.

Sara Paretsky: Oh, you know, it wasn’t a deliberate decision. But she came to me. I was on vacation in Paris, which makes me sound more glamorous than I am. But especially because what happened was that I fell out of bed, which is totally not glamorous. And as I was rubbing my sore hip, I was thinking, what would happen if V.I. got to be my age, seventy-something, and injured herself and could no longer race around the streets after bad guys? And then I thought, I really don’t want V.I. to be old and creaky. I want her to stay kind of fifty-ish.

And really, in that moment, Lily came to me with her name, Lily, this ex-CIA agent who now was on the run from the CIA. The whole storyline took years to develop, and many false starts, but that was how it happened.

LWH: Is Lily going to be a recurring character?

SP: I hope so. You know, everything depends on my being able to write faster than I do because I’m under contract to do a new book in the V.I. series. I wrote 10,000 words that I threw out. I wrote ten thousand more words and threw out eight thousand. But I’ve started a file on Lily. I have a storyline that I’m really excited about for her that is totally hers. It’s not the kind of thing V.I. would be involved with.

LWH: I was wondering since Lily and V.I are both in Chicago, whether there’d ever be a crossover or meetup.

SP: That’s a delicate question. I don’t know if I should say this or not. I mean, I don’t know if this is politically advisable to say this, but Disney owns the rights in perpetuity to V.I. and any characters that hover around her. So, I want to own Lily, and that means that much as I would like to have a lot of crossover, that’s just not going to happen.

LWH: Okay, and Disney has the rights because of the movie? (The 1991 film V.I. Warshawski, starring Kathleen Turner.)

SP: Yes, exactly. And I was young, ignorant, relied on advice. It wasn’t great advice, and here I am.

LWH: Do you feel more of a kinship to Lily than you do to V.I. since you’re both in your seventies?

SP: When V.I. and I were the same age, I don’t think I felt a kinship with her. I was thinking about that this morning. I have a cousin who’s my age, whom I admire greatly. I love her. She’s a wonderful woman in every way. She’s kind of more like V.I. She just got back from backpacking, carrying a thirty-pound backpack through the Boundary Waters in northern Minnesota, and she’s done many wonderful things in her life for women, so I admire her and I admire V.I. in that way.

But I have to say that I actually actively envy Lily. I would like to be Lily. I never wanted to be V.I. I’d like to be that person who could insert herself into groups the way she did when she was actively working as a CIA agent. She scampers up and down mountains. She bathes naked with local women under the full moon and the glacier waters in the country where she worked.

And I mean, like V.I., she takes a lot of risks, but unlike V.I., she’s a team player to a certain extent, insofar as the CIA lets her have a team, and then she’s got these incredible linguistic gifts, so I would like to be Lily, whereas I don’t want to be my cousin. I just like to admire my cousin.

LWH: And you had to create an entirely fictional country for Lily to have had her adventures in.

SP: Yes, I realized if I was going to write a book that was set in the CIA world, sort of set in the CIA world, if I wrote about any of the things that the CIA has really been involved with, I would spend the rest of my life answering letters from people who said, “Well, you got this detail on, and I was there from 1950 to 1990,” and so I thought, okay, the way around that is to create my own country, and then created my own language.

That was a mistake because when the audio recorder was doing the reading, they said there are sixty words in the Hayali language that are in the book that they needed to know how to pronounce. And I’m looking at them and thinking, why did I create a language that was Qs, Zs, and Ws? I don’t know how to pronounce these words. Figure it out yourself. But anyway, I made a stab at it, and I thought, well, if I ever do that again, it’s going to be a language that looks like French.

LWH: You could have made Lily a retired CIA agent who doesn’t have a lot of health issues. She doesn’t have a bum shoulder. But you gave her things that people in their seventies would be going through. Is that just to make it more realistic?

SP: Well, yes, and you know it’s sort of a reflection of my own lived experience. I feel lucky to be in as good shape as I am with eighty kind of lurking around the corner, but I was badly injured in a car crash some years ago, and I have residual problems that keep me from scampering up and down mountains, and I just think if you get to be my age and you don’t have arthritis or joint issues or something that’s slowing you down, you have lived a lucky life.

So, I wanted that lived experience to be something that people could relate to as much as I relate to it, or in the same way that I relate to it. We all have these issues that we’re dealing with, and yet people carry on. And I think that was what I wanted to do with Lily to show that you can just keep on keeping on, even when it’s not so easy.

LWH: When you started writing the V.I. series, you and she were roughly about the same age, but you’ve made her age a lot slower than the rest of us mortals.

SP: Right. It’s just one of her superpowers. I had no imagination about what that series would be. I didn’t know it was going to be a series. I wanted to create a woman detective who was sort of turning the tables on the standard roles for women in crime fiction forty-plus years ago.

I thought I would write this book and then I would go back to whatever else I was doing in my life, which at that time was selling computers to insurance agents. I don’t know if I would have made different decisions if I’d imagined that there would be twenty-three more books about V.I. coming down the pike.

I’m not sure when you’re thirty that you can imagine seventy. I looked at my mother who had terrible health issues. She was in her fifties then, and I thought, oh well, you know, it’s just a question of taking care of yourself. And then I got to be fifty and had my own issues. Life gives you these slaps in the face to tell you to stop being so arrogant.

LWH: Why do you think it was important to have Lily suffering from some of the physical ailments that she does versus making her full of vim and vigor and in great physical shape?

SP: Well, I want a character who readers can connect to. I think everyone second-guesses themselves. Everyone makes choices that they may look back on with regret, as Lily does. She’s thinking back over her long life of service and realizing that there were things that she just didn’t see. They were going on in front of her and she didn’t see them.

I hope people can see their own experience in her, even if their experiences are, I don’t know, in a small town in the Midwest, as opposed to hiking up and down mountains in Central Asia. They’ll see that fundamentally she’s the same kind of person they are and if she can achieve her aspirations, other people can achieve their own aspirations.

LWH: What can you do with a the character in her seventies that you couldn’t or wouldn’t be able to do with with V.I.?

SP: One reason that I took a break from V.I. was that she was getting to be too much like me. Too worried, too feeling overwhelmed by responsibility, too much questioning her judgment. V.I. is supposed to be a lot more—I don’t know if carefree is the right word, but bold. V.I. is supposed to be bolder.

Lily is effective, but she’s not bold in that way. She’s someone who is more emotionally akin to me, I would say. And I was letting V.I. get too much into that space, and it was—I don’t want to say destroying her as a character, but it was making her character less what I wanted her to be. Bringing Lily on board and letting her have that part of my emotional landscape now makes it possible to have V.I revert more to what should be her character.

LWH: Does Lily being as old as she is make her sort of invisible to people and let her go about her skullduggery or whatever she needs to get done?

SP: Yes. There is no disguise like being an old woman in America. I’ll tell you one of the things that I loved about Grace and Frankie in the first episode with Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, is they’re in a liquor store and they cannot get the attention of the person behind the counter because he’s talking to some young person and he just doesn’t register two old women and so they shoplift. It’s like: why not?

LWH: There are going to be readers who read that Sara Peretsky has a new novel out, but they might be upset that it’s not another V.I. story. Do you think there’s going to be appeal, that people are going to enjoy reading both characters, both series?

SP: Well, I hope so. I mean, I’ve had very good feedback from the people who read the book so far. It was published September twenty-four in England. They usually publish the same month as my American publishers, but for some reason they were two months ahead or six weeks ahead. But they sold out their first printing the first week it was on sale, so that that’s encouraging that English readers were willing to take the chance on a new character.

LWH: There are many novelists who have died but their characters keep going. Robert Parker, his Spenser novels are still being written by other people, but Sue Grafton said no, the alphabet ends with Y. What is your thinking? What is your preference?

SP: Oh, I’m with Sue on that. You know, this is my voice. This is my presence in the world. V.I. is too much part of my life, and I feel the same way about Lily. There are other people who write better than I do. There are other people who write faster, more creatively, but it wouldn’t be my voice.

Years ago, the Japanese took over the Macallan whisky company. I was talking to one of the master distillers in the Highlands, and he said that that Suntory was bringing him over to be their lead tester on their chemically created version of Highland whisky, and he said, “They have the Scottish water, they have the Scottish peat, they have the Scottish barley, but they don’t have the Scottish air, and it is not Scotch.”

That’s how I feel about my character. You might have the storyline, you might have the name, but you don’t have my spirit, and so it is not V.I.

L. Wayne Hicks is a freelance writer who covered real-life crimes for newspapers in Florida and Colorado, and has written profiles of many mystery writers including Sara Paretsky, Michael Connelly, John Dunning, Donald J. Sobol, and Stephen White.

#7718. Marisa de los Santos on John Green, detectives, and switching genres as a writer

John Green wrote this: “I fell asleep the way you fall in love, slowly and then all at once.”

I treasure this quotation because it applies to so many changes and revelations, and it happens to be a really good description of how I fell into writing crime fiction. After a career built mostly on upmarket fiction or women’s fiction or book club fiction or whatever term is meant to describe books mostly about relationships, mostly by women, I’ve switched genres. Forever? Not sure. For now? Absolutely. Does it feel momentous? Kind of, yes. How did it happen? Slowly and then all at once.

I’ve wanted to write detective fiction for a very long time. Years. As a reader, I devour it. For well over a decade, when someone asked me to list my favorite living writers, Tana French was one of the first names out of my mouth. She still is. In my mind, she’s the gold standard, but there are many other crime writers on the list, writers of the kind of book you read and immediately say, “God, I wish I’d written that.”

Why? When I think about this question, I run into that thing where you try to explain why you love something that feels so natural and second nature to love that you’re at a loss. It must be due in part to the way I’m fascinated by puzzles: word, jigsaw, logic, riddles, any knotty problem that doesn’t have to do with numbers.

I’m drawn to intricately put-together things that also seem seamless. Poetry is like that, which is maybe why I started out as a poet. There’s a mystery at the heart of every good poem, a thing to unlock, language that flings open a window to a fresh view of what it is to be a person in the world. The tangled and cryptic made beautifully or tragically or terrifyingly clear.

Also, I love crime fiction for the way it can mop its characters into the darkest corners and then force them to find their way out. Characters in detective fiction confront humanity at its most broken, and sometimes that humanity is their own.

I’m especially fascinated by the perspective of the detectives, people whose life’s work is predicated on people hurting other people, whether it’s out of fear, jealousy, personal gain, desperation, or what can only be called evil. Imagine making a pact with the world to stare down what most of us try to avoid, evil and destruction, and to try to hold to account the people who have the audacity to hurt, to murder their fellow human beings.

Detectives pick a side in a way that most of us never have to and they do their best to keep their feet firmly planted on the ground of right and just, even when that ground shakes under them.

So why didn’t I write a crime novel ages ago? There are two reasons.

Firstly, I’ve never had a lot of choice about what I write. I’ve never been a writer with loads of book ideas or one that says, with deliberation, “I want to write X next.” There’s usually a single idea that comes out of the kind of nowhere that’s really everywhere: newspapers, encounters on the street, an overheard conversation, a weirdly blue sky or the way the light hits someone’s face. So many tiny glimmers and slivers that eventually coalesce into an idea.

I write what I’m given to write. I hate how woo-woo that sounds, but oh well. That’s the way it is.

And secondly, I didn’t have a character. Nearly everything I’ve ever written begins with a character, one that lives and develops inside my head, sometimes for years. For me, the story emerges from the characters, not the other way around. And for a long time, I didn’t have a detective character, even though I really, really wanted one.

But to get to the “slowly” part from the John Green quotation, when I look at my books that weren’t mysteries, I see that they were. There’s a mystery at the center of each of them and, in some of them, there’s a character who is actively seeking to solve that mystery.

A boy looking for his biological father. A young woman trying to discover the history of the house she’s inherited. A woman seeking out, however reluctantly, the person who set a fire that threw her world into heartbreak. Two sisters trying to uncover lost years of their mother’s life before it’s too late.

Detectives who aren’t detectives. Mysteries that aren’t murders. Clues to follow. Red herrings. Scraps and shards and dark corners and someone taking the measure of human cruelty or courage or grief or love and picking a side.

Which brings us to the “all at once” part: Lina Cordova. My detective. Well, one of two. Aaron Cash would show up a little later (God, I love that guy). But Lina came first. She arrived suddenly and then lived inside my head until she became a full-fledged person to me. Where did she come from? Beats me. Why then and not before? No idea. But I was super happy to see her.

Lina is half-Filipina, half-white, like me. She has a Filipino doctor father, like me. She is fiercely in love with her people, her dogs, her home. So am I. But she’s not me. She’s way taller, for one thing. And worlds braver. I learned her like you learn a language, slowly then all at once. Before I could write her story, I had to become Lina-fluent. So that’s what I did. It was awesome.

She had the same best friend, Helly, from childhood, through elementary, middle, high school, through college and Lina’s law school years, and into adulthood. Then, someone murdered Helly and that person was never held to account and Lina’s heart and her whole being cracked.

For a long time, she lost herself. So, as so many of us do, she took her shattered self and her family home, to the small city of Sheppley, Pennsylvania, where she found herself again, and she became a cop. One whose ace in the hole is her dead best friend, the voice inside her head that pushes her, sometimes relentlessly, toward the truth. Lina talks to Helly and Helly talks back and of course it’s not really Helly, but, for Lina, it is.

Lina is a mother. She has a teenage daughter and a son on the autism spectrum. She has an ex-husband named Joe, who is still her safe harbor in every storm. She has a dead mother she adores and a father with whom she and her kids live and who is grumpy and bossy and as solid as a lighthouse on a rock. She is drawn to pretty clothes and excellent coffee. She comes home each day to an old stone house, warm yellow light, kids doing homework, two Yorkies, the smell of her dad’s cooking, and peace.

I like an edgy, brooding, jaded, teetering-on-the edge-of-some-personal-chasm-or-other detective as much as the next person, but that’s not Lina. (It’s not Aaron, either, despite his past, the sort people are lucky to get out of alive).

Lina has her frailties: at one point, she calls herself a “soft-boiled detective” and she’s right. No emotional armor, no cynicism. She can’t help but think of even the worst criminals as not monsters but human, a fact that can make her job extremely hard and that also functions as her superpower. She’s the kind of person who watches a pregnant fox cross a road in front of her and feels so protective of it she could weep. She’s funny and piercingly smart. She is haunted, hunted like a fox by hounds, by the cases she left unsolved.

All at once, I had Lina. And then, I had Aaron. And then, from these two people, all at once, I had The Trusted. Because in that way the world of crime fiction is like the world of any other fiction, at least for me, a place where the story emerges from the characters, spins itself into being out of who they are: their personal histories, all their little quirks and preferences and weirdness, their friendships, all their passions, the books they read, the food they eat, everything that scares or sustains them.

Thanks for showing up, Lina. You, too, Aaron. Thank you to all my earlier books and the characters who allowed them to happen. It turns out, at long last, slowly then all at once, I got to be a crime writer after all.

Marisa de los Santos is the New York Times bestselling author of Love Walked In, Belong to Me, The Trusted, and Falling Together. She has also published a poetry collection called From the Bones Out.
