#7717. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7716. No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Staton v. Jefferson Health-Abington, decided by Judge Harvey Bartle (E.D. Pa.) Oct. 15, but just noted a few days ago in the Westlaw Bulletin:

[Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so. She relies on a document entitled "Patient Specimen Release Form" which she signed on August 22, 2021. In her prayer for relief, plaintiff seeks the award of "compensatory and consequential damages against [Jefferson] … in an amount to be determined at trial, based on the unique personal, cultural and spiritual value of Ms. Staton's placenta." In addition, she asks the court to "[g]rant such other and further relief as the Court deems just, equitable, and proper." …

In Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract. The parties have cited no case and this court has found none where the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania has ever held that emotional distress damages are recoverable in a breach of contract action. However, in D'Ambrosio, v. Pennsylvania National Mutual Casualty Insurance Co. (1981) the Court left the door open….:

The possibility cannot be ruled out that emotional distress damages may be recoverable on a contract where, for example, "the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result." …

[Restatement (Second) of Contracts §] 353, which the Pennsylvania Supreme Court referenced by a different number in D'Ambrosio, precludes emotional damages except in very limited circumstances:

Recovery for emotional disturbance will be excluded unless the breach also caused bodily harm or the contract or the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result.

The Restatement gives examples in Comment a. of cases which fit into the second exception. They are contracts for the proper disposition of a dead body, contracts for the carriage of messages concerning death, and contracts of carriers and innkeepers with passengers and guests….

In this court's view, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would follow the general rule that emotional damages are not recoverable in contract cases…. While contracts for the proper disposition of dead bodies allow for distress damages under § 353, plaintiff concedes that she "does not equate a placenta with a decedent's remains."

In opposing to the pending motion, plaintiff stresses her allegations that her placenta had personal, cultural, and spiritual value to her and that she suffered emotional distress when it was not returned to her. Even if true, her subjective reaction to the alleged breach of contract is not relevant to the issue before the court. In Pennsylvania, emotional distress damages are generally not recoverable in a breach of contract action. Whether emotional distress damages would ever be recoverable would depend on the type of contract or breach alleged, not on the plaintiff's emotional or mental state.

The standard set forth in § 353 is an objective one. No case suggests that the application of § 353 or the allowance of emotional distress damages would be decided based on the effect of the breach on the particular plaintiff without regard to the type of contract or breach involved. Otherwise, the floodgates would be open to emotional distress damages in virtually every breach of contract action….

The result might in principle have been different in a tort lawsuit for conversion, since emotional distress damages are generally available in such torts; but it's not clear that ejected parts of the body such as the placenta would be treated as property under Pennsylvania law for conversion purposes.

Joseph Hoynoski and Jeffrey Chomco (Marshall Dennehey, P.C.) represent defendants.

#7715. Slow Horses has been renewed well into the future

Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone

Yes. Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed. Season 6 just aired this fall, on its home network of Apple TV+, and work on the 7th season has begun.

But the series has been renewed even further than that. When Season 6 aired, we learned that the show had been renewed for an 8th season. This was great news.

And now, Apple has announced that the series will continue through Season 10! Yes, Seasons 9 and 10 have been announced! This means we have four more seasons to look forward to. That’s four more years of Jackson Lamb and his crew of misfits. That’s a whole American presidential term’s worth of Slow Horses.

Until Season 6, each season of the show has adapted a single one of Heron’s novels, all in chronological order. Season 6 broke the mold by adapting two: the sequential volumes Joe Country and Slough House. This means there are two extant novels left to adapt, Bad Actors and Clown Town, and early reports have confirmed that seasons 7 and 8 will undertake each of those novels, respectively. This means that Heron’s next novel will also be guaranteed a season, as will the next.

Will he indeed write more? Yes, it certainly seems so, though there have been no announcements about a new installment. The most recent novel, Clown Town, was released in 2025, and Heron’s novels typically have a 1-3 year gap in between them. But there’s still plenty of relevant Slough House material rife for adaptation; Heron has also published five Slough House novellas, none of which have been adapted yet. (Interested readers should note that all the novellas thus far have been collected in a volume called Standing By the Wall.)

The series Slow Horses stars Gary Oldman as the irascible, perpetually-disheveled, foul-mouthed, flatulent and yet thoroughly lovable MI5 agent Jackson Lamb, who oversees a notorious departmental backwater of the Secret Service called Slough House, an institutional repository for agents who have badly messed up (or pissed off somebody important). Time and time again Lamb and his team of oddballs, including Jack Lowden’s put-in-Slough-House-by-sabotage River Cartwright, wind up using their special skills, disregard for the rules, and occasional desire to prove themselves/not be messed with to save the day, often. It’s the best.

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. #7714. The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

Chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

Satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each new matter at the outset?

Chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of new datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material issues in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or issue. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

Satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every new tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

Ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

Chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our new law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

Satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

Chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same plan from the outset.

Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

Satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client says it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”

Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

Chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati said earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

Satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

Chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely important, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

Satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be said in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

Chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

#7713. Journal of Free Speech Law: "An Unsettling Agreement: Meta, Jawboning, and the First Amendment," by Evelyn Douek

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The first in a series of articles we'll be publishing over the next few months from our Free Speech and the Meta Settlement symposium.

The settlement agreement that Meta reached with state Attorneys General in August 2026 is constitutionally unsound. The changes that the AGs pressured Meta to make to its platforms as part of the settlement burden the rights of third parties—Meta's users—in various ways (some content-neutral, some content-based, and some even viewpoint-based), and yet these terms have so far escaped First Amendment scrutiny.

Because these changes are being done under government pressure, the agreement violates the rule against jawboning; Meta's users should therefore be able to bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. Settlement agreements should not be allowed to become a loophole in the First Amendment's protections.

According to the settlement agreement that Meta reached with 52 Attorneys General in August 2026, it is the parties' belief that "the public interest is best served when platforms and regulators work as partners." This may well be true in some, or perhaps even many, cases. But the settlement creates a system of pervasive and invasive speech regulation, and in that context such cooperation might be said to be "startling and dangerous."

First Amendment doctrine stands for the idea that we should generally be suspicious of government power over speech, and specifically ensures that government actors cannot pressure, or partner with, private actors to "do indirectly what [they are] barred from doing directly." That is: the government cannot evade constitutional constraints by enlisting private actors to impose its favored speech rules on its behalf. A settlement agreement is not a First Amendment-free zone, and the terms of Meta's deal with the Attorneys General at the very least need to be subjected to First Amendment scrutiny. This Article argues that because the Settlement Agreement attempts to evade such scrutiny, it is constitutionally unsound.

To make the stakes of this argument clear, imagine an alternate settlement agreement in which Meta, instead of promising changes like age assurance measures and time limits on kids' usage of its platforms, agreed to prohibit all users from seeing political content or (to make the point even more acute) all pro-Democrat content. The dangers of allowing such an agreement to escape constitutional scrutiny seem obvious. But because concern about kids' use of social media is bipartisan—and no doubt in part because kids themselves are often excluded from conversations about their rights—the constitutional infirmities of the Settlement Agreement have generally flown under the radar. But kids have speech rights too, as do the adult users of Meta's platforms who will also be affected by this Agreement, and politicians and platforms cannot constitutionally agree to forgo those rights on others' behalf.

I will argue that the third parties whose speech rights are burdened by the Settlement Agreement can bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the Agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. This is true for settlement agreements that create such burdens on third-party rights in general, because any other conclusion would allow settlement agreements to become a loophole officials could use to regulate speech without facing constitutional scrutiny. And, as applied to this Settlement Agreement in particular, a large number of its provisions may well fail to survive constitutional scrutiny. Many of the content-neutral requirements in the Agreement mirror mandates that states have attempted to impose through legislation in recent years, and while these laws are still working their way through the courts and the case outcomes are mixed, the majority of decisions have enjoined similar requirements as violating the First Amendment. There are also content- and viewpoint-based requirements in the Agreement that are aimed at influencing what kids see online that would almost certainly fail First Amendment scrutiny if enacted as law.

Considering the Settlement Agreement against this backdrop throws into sharp relief exactly why the First Amendment has rules to ensure that the government cannot avoid constitutional scrutiny by regulating speech through means other than legislation. This fact may be deeply frustrating to some. We are now around a decade into the "techlash" against social media platforms. Despite all these years of concern and debate, the law and politics of platform regulation have made legislative solutions elusive. Attempts to reimagine First Amendment doctrine to give states more leeway to regulate the internet have failed.

There might be a temptation, therefore, to think of the Agreement as an overdue reckoning that cleverly overcomes these obstacles and finally brings Big Tech's worst offender to heel. Indeed, it may only be the start of the reckoning: A month after Meta agreed to settle, TikTok entered into a settlement with Alabama that is clearly modeled on the Meta Settlement Agreement. States are bringing lawsuits against artificial intelligence companies using the same theories as in the Meta case that led to the Settlement. States may think they have found a new way of achieving their regulatory objectives that does not require passing any laws at all.

But the First Amendment does not permit the government to evade review by simply changing the instrument of regulation. Otherwise, its protections would be paper-thin. And as frustrating as the government may find the commands of the First Amendment, they are a feature and not a bug of the American constitutional system. It is imperative that courts make clear that settlement agreements are not one neat trick to evade these constraints, lest states conclude they can abandon the hard and important work of building political will and legislative capacity for more comprehensive legal solutions, and instead regulate through one constitutionally infirm settlement at a time.

This Article proceeds as follows. Part I shows how the Settlement Agreement creates burdens on the speech rights of third parties: namely, Meta's users. Part II, the crux of the Article, argues that given these burdens, the Settlement Agreement violates the broad rule against what is known as jawboning—governmental pressure on private actors to restrict the speech of others. Part III takes a step back from the doctrinal landscape and considers what the Settlement Agreement suggests about the reduced ambitions and disappointments of debates about platform regulation.

How to effectively regulate new and fast-changing technologies continues to be one of the most pressing challenges of our time. Our regulatory solutions must respect the rights of society at large and not merely reflect the interests of the tech companies and the politicians that regulate them. The First Amendment is one essential safeguard in ensuring this is the case.

#7712. A Study In Red, White and Blue: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in the USA

When I was choosing the setting for my new book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.

Holmes, for all his fantastical adventures, rarely travelled beyond London, glimpsing the wider world only when it came to his doorstep. Professor Moriarty, presumed dead post-Reichenbach and presumably still notorious in the UK, is in the exact opposite position.

He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.

While I was scouring the globe for an interesting place to send the master criminal, I kept coming back to a recurring theme in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s books. Indeed, even as a child, reading the classic Holmes adventures, one thought kept jumping out at me…

As I grew up, I discovered just how true this is. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s enthusiasm with the United States was a matter of public record. He took great inspiration from this newfound nation, recovering from a civil war and forging its future before his eyes.

In the process of looking into this transatlantic fascination, I thought I’d share some weird and wonderful findings about Doyle’s brushes with the states, his encounters with citizens of that nation…  and one confrontation with a visitor from Atlantis.

Even before he set foot in the States, Doyle devoured news from America. In fact, factions and societies from the USA featured prominently throughout his work and across the Sherlock Holmes canon.

When he was just twenty-one years old, Doyle anonymously published “An American’s Tale”, a short story in which an Englishman is accused of murdering a rival in Arizona. Taking the Englishman to “Flytrap Gulch” to hang him for his crime, the supposed victim is unexpectedly discovered inside… a giant man-eating plant.

One of Doyle’s more fantastical tales, it certainly paints the USA as a strange and undiscovered country.

As he embarked on the Holmes canon, Doyle still injected America into his stories, with a particular interest in the factions and societies across the pond.

His story, “The Five Orange Pips” features allusions to the infamous KKK. His final of the Sherlock Holmes novels, The Valley of Fear, was born out of his fascination with the Molly Maguires, a secret society that engaged in radical industrial action against Pennsylvanian mining companies, and the Pinkertons, the brutal detective agency who were hired to stop them.

Doyle’s enthusiasm for American goings-on did sometimes outpace his knowledge, however, particularly due to his reliance on secondary sources which filtered to the UK.

Holmes’ very first appearance, A Study In Scarlet, featured an organisation called the Danites, an avenging division of the Mormon Church’s mysterious “Council of Four”.

While the Danites certainly existed, historians consider them a short-lived faction based in mid-century Missouri, and far from the organised assassin squad from the book, with Doyle’s own daughter explaining that her father “would be the first to admit that his first Sherlock Holmes novel was full of errors about the Mormons”.

For the record, there’s no evidence that he believed in man-eating plants.

Eventually, shortly after Sherlock met his end at the Reichenbach Falls, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle finally visited America for the first time.

The Sherlock Holmes stories had proceeded him. He was met with an incredible reception from his already prominent U.S. fanbase, with the Boston Globe reporting him as; well proportioned, attractive and with a handsome face.

In his journeys, Arthur Conan Doyle only grew fonder of America; reporting an incredible time spent on an elevator in Manhattan’s Woolworth Building, whose speed he compared to an artillery weapon, and defending the USA against nitpicking critics by saying;

“Every globe-trotter has paragraphs about the number of spittoons in a hotel bar (as if it matters!)”

Doyle also fell in love with the sport of baseball, to the point of committing a cardinal sin for any Brit; suggesting British football teams should adopt the sport.

“I will venture to say, that if this was done, we should in a few years have as many to see a baseball final between Tottenham Hotspur and Preston North End as come now to the football.

As to the furore which a decent British team, could we evolve one, would create in America, it is impossible to exaggerate it.”

Sadly, the United Kingdom has failed to assemble Doyle’s dream team.

Despite the international success of his books, it was his forays into Spiritualism which brought Doyle back to the United States in the 1920’s, and which brought him in contact with his most prominent trans-atlantic friendship.

One of the dramas that marked Doyle’s later American travels was his fractious friendship with magician Harry Houdini.

Admirers of each other’s work, Doyle and Houdini held the opposite opinions on the supernatural that one might expect. Doyle, the creator of super-logician Sherlock Holmes, had become a devout spiritualist, while the magician Houdini was an ardent sceptic.

Strangely enough, so strong was Doyle’s belief, that he insisted Houdini’s escapist tricks involved some form of magic, refusing to budge when Houdini himself told him otherwise.

“My dear chap.” Doyle wrote in a letter to his friend. “Why do you go around the world seeking a demonstration of the occult when you are giving one all the time?”

Houdini even invited Doyle to the annual dinner at the Society of American Magicians. As a prank, and to prove Magicians could be fooled as much as they claimed Spiritualists were, Doyle screened footage of “live dinosaurs” to an astounded audience.

These live dinosaurs would prove to be stop-motion animations, taken from the upcoming film adaptation of Doyle’s novel; The Lost World.

Despite their spirited back and forth, tensions between the pair came to a head during a 1922 visit to Atlantic City, where Doyle’s wife Jean, channelled Houdini’s mother at a séance. The incident forced Houdini to publicly denounce the events in question, placing Doyle & Houdini publicly at odds.

It was on his Spiritualism tour that Doyle had the strangest encounter Doyle he would perhaps have in America, when Doyle met one of his fans, an old Colonel from the South.

While in Cleveland, described unflatteringly by Doyle as “a grim city of iron and shipping”, Doyle was advancing his lectures on Spiritualism, when he was confronted by an old Southern Colonel with an incredible story to tell.

“The Colonel thought he was an Atlantean by origin,” Doyle reported, with the Colonel continuing to explain that his mother was the former Atlantean Queen.

Though the author tolerated this eccentric visitor in the daytime, when the Colonel showed up at his hotel room at night, with a message from the former Queen, Doyle was forced to confront the more troubling side of fandom.

In the end, long after Doyle’s love-affair with the USA began, Sherlock Holmes himself finally set foot in the States.

It was in 1917, in “The Final Bow”, the last story in the Sherlock Holmes canon, that the detective confirmed he had crossed the Atlantic, travelling to Chicago and beyond.

It’s a fitting end to a canon which, despite taking place primarily in London, is so deeply suffused with Doyle’s love for the States.

The more I’ve learned about it, the more of a privilege it has seemed, to get the chance to send the iconic Professor to 1890’s New York.

A place full of the societies, mysticism and people his creator adored so much, where he’ll pull in to the same dock that Sir Arthur Conan Doyle did when he first set foot in America.

Jack Anderson is a UK-based writer of horror and mystery fiction. Jack got his start writing for the internet, penning the viral serial "Has Anyone Heard of the Left/Right Game?," which he wrote in a caffeine-fueled haze. It has since been adapted into a hit QCODE podcast starring Tessa Thompson in the leading role of Alice. His debut thriller, The Grief Doctor, was published by Raven Books in June 2024. Jack is also developing a number of original television and film ideas across the horror genre. He lives with his wife in Sheffield. Lifelong fans of games and puzzles, together they’re burning through every escape room in the North of England.

#7711. Further Discussion of Whether Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Is Based on a "Misquote"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A podcast discussion of my blogpost, John Bash's critique of a controversial NYT story, and the NYT's response to criticism.

I recently appeared on an episode of the Reload podcast, hosted by Reload founder and editor Stephen Gutowski, to discuss my blog post taking aim at the New York Times story alleging current Second Amendment jurisprudence is based upon a "misquote" of Blackstone.

As noted in my original post, the NYT story was harshly criticized by attorney John Bash, a former clerk to Justice Scalia during the term Heller was decided who was interviewed (but not quoted) in the story. As also noted in that post, the Times issued a response to my post. As discussed in the podcast, I did not find the response particularly persuasive, nor did John Bash.

As I note on the podcast, there are perfectly reasonable arguments that current Second Amendment jurisprudence has gone astray, and that some courts have placed undue weight on the contested passage in the Heller opinion (which did not purport to set out a test). But these are separate questions from whether there was a "misquote" in the Heller opinion. It seems to me the obsession with the latter derives from a desire to discredit contemporary gun rights jurisprudence by suggesting it all stems from a mistake (or worse), rather than by contesting it on the merits.

As for the Blackstone source at issue, just as the Times did not place the contested Heller passage in its full context so that readers could see the point Scalia was making, it did not highlight the full Blackstone passage (other than providing a hyperlink in the web version of the story) or unpack the point Blackstone was making--a point that is arguably even less favorable to gun ownership restrictions than is the relevant passage in Heller.

in his seminal 1769 treatise, "Commentaries on the Laws of England," Blackstone referred to weapons that were "dangerous or unusual," suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted.

The offence of riding or going armed, with dangerous or unusual weapons, is a crime against the public peace, by terrifying the good people of the land; and is particularly prohibited by the statute of Northampton, upon pair of forfeiture of the arms, and imprisonment during the king's pleasure: in like manner as, by the laws of Solon, every Athenian was finable who walked about the city in armour.

Those who want gun rights jurisprudence to hew more closely to Blackstone than does Heller want to be careful what they wish for, as it might not be much authority at all for laws prohibiting the mere possession of unusually dangerous weapons (such as those the Supreme Court will consider this term), as opposed to laws prohibiting the carrying of such arms in ways that could "terrify[]." The Times does not "misquote" Blackstone, but some might conclude the Times was not fairly representing what Blackstone wrote either.

For some additional perspectives on this kerfuffle, see:

Jonathan H. Adler (@jadler1969) is the Tazewell Taylor Professor of Law at the William & Mary Law School and a senior fellow at the Property and Environment Research Center.

#7710. Injunction Against Repeating Defamatory Statements (Including Ones Calling Woman "Witch" and "Satan Servant") + $35M Damages

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

In Life Mastery Network LLC v. Haygarth, by Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.), Life Mastery and Liane Wilson sued Paula Haygarth, Byron Horvath, and Stefanie Vogt-Horvath for various torts. Haygarth et al. ("Counterclaimants") then counterclaimed against Life Mastery and Wilson ("Counterclaim-Defendants") for defamation and false light.

Specifically, the jury found the following statements to be defamatory, some of which were posted on Wilson's Instagram account, and some of which, as indicated, appeared on her website, www.exposingfamilyabuse.com ("Exposing Family Abuse website"):

The jury returned verdicts on August 13, 2026, awarding Byron and Stefanie $1.6 million each. The jury also awarded Paula $1.6 million for the statements found to be defamatory at trial, and awarded an additional $500,000 in damages for the statements the Court found defamatory per se at the summary judgment stage. Counterclaimants were each awarded $10 million in punitive damages. In total, the jury awarded Counterclaimants $35.3 million in damages.

As I mentioned, yesterday the court issued an injunction barring plaintiffs "from repeating the statements already found to be defamatory, and are directed to remove (or direct removal of) the statements already found to be defamatory from the Exposing Family Abuse website." The court noted that such anti-libel injunctions are generally legally permissible (see this article for more details) with regard to specific statements that have been found to be false and defamatory in a final judgment:

In this case, Counterclaimants seek an order enjoining Counterclaim-Defendants from repeating statements that have already found to be defamatory. Such an injunction is narrowly tailored to statements already found to be unprotected by the First Amendment, and thus does not constitute an unlawful prior restraint….

Although the public has a substantial interest in protecting freedom of expression, it also has an interest in protecting individuals against reputational injury caused by defamatory falsehoods. Here, an injunction prohibiting repetition of statements already determined defamatory protects individuals against reputational injury and leaves Counterclaim-Defendants free to engage in other protected speech….

And the court declined to certify to the Hawaii Supreme Court the question whether Hawaii law authorizes such injunctions, concluding that it was sufficiently likely that Hawaii law actually does so authorize:

The Ninth Circuit has provided that certification to a state supreme court is a process that is reserved for state law questions that present significant issues, "including those with important public policy ramifications," and that have not yet been resolved by the state courts…. Certification should be taken only after careful consideration and should not be done so lightly.

Here, the Court finds certification to the Hawai'i Supreme Court to be unnecessary to resolve the present motion. The relief requested concerns either repetitions or removals of speech already found to be defamatory—a category of speech not even Counterclaim-Defendants say is protected under the Hawai'i constitution. Furthermore, the Court agrees with Counterclaimants that the effort to certify such a question would unnecessarily delay entry of final judgment in the matter.

Joseph Adams, Laura Moritz, and Louise Ing (Dentons US LLP) represent the Countclaimants.

#7709. Quinn Connor on body horror, queerness, academia, and southern gothic novels

Your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories. This novel is set at Basin College, a small school in a remote part of Arkansas where Celia Kiel, the school’s archivist, has spent her whole life.

After discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation. Working from a partial manuscript she found pickled in formaldehyde, she teams up with Joan Harriot, a literature postdoc, who is not just a gifted mimic but Celia’s academic nemesis, to forge and reconstruct the book in an effort to save the school.

The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.

The book tells the story of a very dysfunctional pair writing a manuscript, and so we reached out to Dr. Robyn Barrow and Alex Cronin, the writing duo behind Quinn Connor to ask about how they write together without trying to kill each other, academia, queer Southern stories, body horror, and how their writing surprises the people who know them.

AD: I really enjoyed Your Beloved Remains, which was so much fun. Maybe fun is the wrong word?

AD: From the beginning of your writing career, I’m sure people have asked, how do the two of you work together? Here you have written a book that is explicitly about a literary partnership. Was this kind of inevitable?

AC: It probably was a little bit inevitable, because it’s always been interesting to us. Just quickly on the way we work: We’ve been doing this for thirteen years now. The way it works is that I have a character, Robyn has a character, and then we bring them in conversation. We are often literally passing the laptop back and forth, line by line, switching who writes it. So it ends up being super seamless.

Of course, over thirteen years, I think we have learned enough about it to know how bad it could be if we did not truly like each other. We have strong boundaries with co-writing. We get along. We have a lot of the same tastes. We love each other. These are the things that make co-writing safe.

But because it’s so safe for us, it was really fun to explore [the question], “but what if it wasn’t safe?” Because it is so vulnerable to be co-writing and sharing a creative project. To share that can feel really scary. So what if the worst thing happened? What if all of those hurt feelings that could exist grew into something wild and terrifying?

AD: There is a scene where, not to spoil too much, but Celia gets those first pages back and she goes, this is horrible. Because she can’t give or take criticism well. But she’s also in pain because it’s so good and she knows she could never have written it, so she’s overwhelmed by anger and jealousy.

AC: Robyn and I are very lucky because we have similar standards and we have similar but different talents. We’re very compatible, but co-writing with someone who is not compatible would be really difficult. Celia finds herself in this position where she just is struggling to keep up and that is a horror for her because she wants to be the keeper of Beatrice. The keeper of this archive and of her voice. And she can’t do it. The way that Harriot describes it is Celia is “a high priestess who can’t hear the voice of god.”

AD: Which is such a great phrase, but the book resembles a lot of different genres. It’s gothic, it’s dark academia. Robyn, I know you work in academia, so I’m sure you have thoughts on the genre.

RB: We have always loved Donna Tartt and The Secret History. We loved it and around 2017, 2018, it felt like suddenly the internet discovered it. It was everywhere and it sort of ballooned into this whole genre, “dark academia.”

It’s great that there are so many people enjoying reading and writing this genre, but it has gone quite far from The Secret History. Now there’s dark academic fantasy and all these versions that, to me, have nothing to do with academia. They’re not really exploring the themes of the university that I find interesting.

When I pitched the idea for Your Beloved Remains to Alex, I was like, “We’re gonna make this call from inside the house.” This is about academic frustration. The kind of rage that can build up in an eternal grad program.

When I came up with the pitch, I was in the sixth year of an eight-year grad program. A lot of Harriot’s struggles with her career and the feelings that she has about being a postdoc, was cathartic for me to write through. Hopefully it gets back to some of the roots of dark academia. We’re re-coining this book as “academic horror.”

AC: I’m just going to parrot what I’ve heard Robyn say before, which is that often these books focus on the students, but in our book, the students are not really a part of it. It’s about the institution. The students can leave on holiday break. They get to go home. This is about the people that don’t leave. Where the university is their life. Which, for Robyn, has been a really good thing.

RB: It’s funny because since I wrote the book, I have gone on to finish my PhD and get a tenure-track job, which is like winning the lottery. That was never in the cards for Harriot. Harriot was never destined for tenure. [laughs]

AC: It’s kind of the same thing as the collaboration question. It’s an exploration of the dark side and the horrible “what if things had gone a different way.”

AD: There’s an exchange in the book. “What does it mean to want something so much you end up destroying it?” Harriot answers “it sounds like doing a PhD in the humanities.”

RB: [laughs] Exactly! Sometimes you make the thing that you love your job, which I would say is true both in academia and as an author. You make writing that you love the thing that you make money off of, and then you spend so long grinding that you actually ruin it. Harriot is so burnt out. She clearly came to being a literary scholar because she loved reading, and now she’s so cynical and so lost because of all the years of struggle with that.

AD: You said that students are kind of the point of academia, but they’re only there for a few years, but there are people who spend their whole lives there.

RB: Since most people who write books about academia have only ever been undergraduate students, they see themselves as the center of the system. But they’re really the compensatory engine of a system that is producing something that is actually not their education. I think that is fascinating. I truly care so much about my students. My students are the reason I want to be in academia, but for many researchers and faculty members, students are not the reason that they are doing their job.

AC: Also, the people who run the college, the board and the President, they’re looking at the bottom line. There’s this question that’s the propulsive engine of the first act: Is Basin College going to close? Celia cares because of the archive and because it’s her home. But there’s also the question of what about all of these students that are currently there. What’s going to happen to them?

There is this unspoken understanding that the board doesn’t care about them. It’s not about them. They’re a part of this system and nobody is thinking about them at all.

RB: The book was coming out of a moment when it felt like universities were operating as these hedge funds for the wealthy. We started writing this book in 2023. Now higher education is under threat. I think that the university is a really good and important thing in our society. I want to defend it and I want to be a good voice in the university.

AC: I think there’s a big question in the book, “how do you love something?” Celia’s version of loving it is excusing any of its wrongs and pretending it’s perfect. Harriot’s version is critiquing it almost to the point of picking it apart.

I think that’s how we feel about the university. Yes, it’s wonderful. It’s something that we need. It also is worthy of critique and could be improved and made better. There are these questions of how you engage with something that you love, and because you love it you are frustrated by it greatly.

AD: Historically most universities were set apart from cities to let people study and work. And there’s a way that attracts people like Celia who use it as a place to hide from the larger world.

RB: It’s got a monastic quality. That can also go into a cult-like quality. Harriot is really running from her past by arriving at Basin College, which is a very particularly isolated and spooky version.

AD: It is very remote, but also, there are a lot of colleges in the middle of nowhere.

AC: Beatrice Donahue created it specifically for that reason. She said, “my husband is finally dead, I have money, I am free. I want to go do exactly what I want to do.”

What she wanted to do was find some place remote where she and the women in her life and her lover could be themselves in all of their weird, witchy, queer glory. A lot of universities were not created for that reason, but it was fun to think about this university that was and how these things can start from such a seed and still become so institutionalized and twisted and different from the starting place.

RB: I do like that point that Basin College in its foundational message, was meant to be a safe place for women and a safe place for queer people to live as their true selves. I feel like the university can be that way. The ivory tower is a place where you see many different kinds of people getting to ask the kinds of questions they’re interested in. I feel like that is a beautiful thing about college. But it all depends on who’s in charge

AD: It does get at that, which is so important for people. Also it touches on how a lot of schools that may have become institutions, but were started by people who were strange or even crazy.

AC: [laughs] Beatrice is, but she’s gloriously powerful. She’s dead but she has cast such a long shadow. She brought these women who did not fit in society. One of our inspirations was Victorian tea rooms, which was one of the few jobs back then that women could have. So Beatrice had a tea room. Women were finding ways to exist and to be free under incredible constraints. That’s what Basin College was for her.

AD: It’s a queer book about how queer spaces have always existed just as queer people have always existed. And that these spaces and institutions have existed through time.

RB: This is our third novel and in our previous work we’ve had queer storylines that have been a reclaiming of queer joy, which has been really wonderful. In this book we wanted to just have freaky scary lesbians doing bad things and not apologizing for it. Just ripping the world down.

AC: There’s all sorts of different ways that queer people can be portrayed. Because they’re people. You almost have to start with a portrayal where they are good, because there are a lot of people that may not have knowingly met a queer person. You almost have to start with, guess what, you can love a queer character. The more these stories come out, the more freedom you have to add grittiness and reality into that portrayal.

It’s wonderful to be able to have queer characters that behave badly and it doesn’t feel like a condemnation on queerness as an entire experience. For us, being able to write through queer joy gave us the freedom to write queer messiness as well.

RB: This is coming from our background as Southern women, as well. I feel like up in these parts it can feel that queer pain is a distant memory for many people, but for us, coming out in 2018 was a completely different world. Writing Southern stories about queer people means a lot to people in Arkansas and these places.

AC: There’s people that would have you believe that queerness doesn’t exist there. Or that it needs to be kept very quiet, or regulated extremely heavily. Or made illegal. But there have always been queer people in Arkansas.

There’s also the idea that the North is the home of the ivory tower. That New England is where you’ve got all these schools, but there’s always been incredible intelligence like in Arkansas. These things, that they would have you believe don’t exist, have always been there. These people, that they tell you don’t exist or don’t deserve to exist, have always been there and been a part of it.

AD: As you were talking about the messiness, I keep thinking about how the book takes place over a few months. It opens with the fall semester and the school is functioning as it has been, and by the Christmas holiday, everything unravels and descends into chaos.

RB: We have Beatrice Donahue’s dark secret at the center of the novel. You don’t find out right away, which has made it hard for me at times to know how to pitch the novel. I feel like this is a key element that you don’t want to spoil. Beatrice lost her lover and the aftermath of that grief and where she goes with that is super kinky and interesting and transgressive and queer.

Then you have these women in the 1980s that are excavating that and discovering within themselves how they feel about that and how they feel about each other. It’s fun to surprise the reader with that part way through. It’s good to highlight for readers that the book is spicy and bizarre. And a great time, hopefully.

AC:  We’re thinking about all of these highfalutin ideas, but we’re also playing a game of chicken with each other. We’re trying to freak each other out a little bit when we’re writing. We’re trying to make it fun.

Sometimes I write something and then I’m sitting there waiting for Robin to get to it so I can get her reaction. There’s a lot about the book that is intentionally fun because we were having fun. Everything that the reader feels, we felt as we were writing it and surprising each other and grossing each other out and delighting each other.

AD: I’m sure. Going, what if she cuts her foot, what if it gets infected, what if we have this body horror scene.

AC: What’s weird is that we wrote all of that, but it grosses me out to think about it. One of my friends was reminding me about a particular scene with the foot. I remember us writing that, and I have not gone back and read it again because it grosses me out! [laughs]

AD: I’m pretty sure I know the exact scene you’re talking about.

AC: [laughs] It’s a weird way to feel about something you wrote.

AD: At the center of the book is this lost manuscript of Beatrice’s, and in writing the book you had to figure out how much of that book to write, how much to include so it doesn’t overwhelm the story.

AC: A couple people have asked about this, actually. One friend said, “you should do Dreams of the Rose, the entire book from Beatrice Donahue.” Our answer has consistently been, “no!” My gosh, that was so hard to do.

RB: One of the big influences in the book that I don’t think we’ve talked about before is Possession by A.S. Byatt. I love that novel. It’s absolutely amazing. In that book there’s a lot of the writing of the authors in the book.

With Beatrice Donahue we wanted the kind of unreachability of her to be center stage. What’s on the page is all of the writings of Beatrice Donahue that there is. There’s no additional pages. We found it extremely tiresome to do.

Harriot has this power of mimicry where she can hear the writing of someone else and then produce it. That came from my own perception of my own writing. I feel like I can really get the sound of someone else’s writing and copy that or produce that, in a sense. Beatrice Donahue is a shared character, but I would read Mary Shelley and Poe and nineteenth-century work and then I would write these passages of Donahue.

I’m very attuned to word choice. I feel like it’s so easy to get taken out of that kind of writing with a misplaced word or something that just doesn’t hit quite right. This is just someone in the present pretending to write about the past. I wanted it to have a strong truth claim. Starting with the note from the editors and then all the writing, I wanted it to feel really immersive. This could have been true.

AD: You mentioned before that each were the primary writer of one of the characters. Who did you write?

AC: I wrote Celia. To the great surprise of most people, I wrote Celia.

RB: For some reason, Alex’s friends were like, “she couldn’t have done that.”

AC: I think because the wildness of Celia and where we go in her perspective is pretty stark. I think that a lot of people that know me are just surprised because I’m an introvert. There’s a lot that comes out in Celia’s perspective that people maybe didn’t think we were capable of, who have read our other books or know us personally.

AD: I think Celia would have to be written by an introvert.

AC: That’s how I feel! She’s got a very rich inner world, and it’s twisted in there.

AD: It’s also funny that you wrote the foot scene and then went, this is disgusting, I can’t read it again.

RB: Alex writes way grosser stuff than I do.

AD: That is interesting. Do people have a somewhat misunderstood sense of what you write or how you write?

RB: I think there’s definitely a pattern between the three books. Alex’s characters are always extremely vulnerable and very emotionally open. Which is interesting because between the two of us, she’s definitely more emotionally unavailable in the real world. My characters are a bit more closed off and they’re usually cool. [laughs] I’m the least cool person, but then I write these cool characters. To my best friends, it’s pretty obvious that Harriot is me. She’s like my shadow side.

People do have a good time guessing. We go back and forth, should we tell people who wrote what? Should we keep it a secret? Because obviously we want the experience to be seamless.

AD: You mentioned one struggle has been finding a way to talk about the book without spoiling too much. Which I understand.

RB: I’ve been thinking about the pitch for the book and if we’re pitching it correctly. I think what it’s really about is that Celia longs for more than anything, the love of this Victorian author that she’s always admired. In her desperate reaching for that, she recruits her academic nemesis who has this talent for mimicry to go with her on this journey that leads to a total shit show descent into complete chaos in this snowy remote college.

That’s what I think the book is about. There’s many, many bizarre and spicy surprises along the way. [laughs]

AD: It’s true, and a lot of what we’ve been talking about, the gothic elements and academia and the two falling for each other, that’s the first half. The second half, just buckle up for the ride.

RB: Someone asked us, do you provide aftercare for your readers at the end of the book? I was like, we don’t. I feel like the book is just like a rock and roll roller coaster and you get spat out at the end. I hope that you’re sitting there, staring at the book going, what did I just read? [laughs]

Alex Dueben has written for The Believer, Vulture, The Millions, The Los Angeles Review of Books, The Brooklyn Rail, and many other publications. He is the writer and editor of the artist monograph Hurricane Nancy, and his debut novel is forthcoming.

#7708. After Weil Gotshal’s collapse, law firm merger interest heats up

Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock)

The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

“Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”

“A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

“The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s important to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith said to Law.com.

Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

“We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith said. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s important to look at their options early.”
